RustStream 是如何构建的，以及它的设计让服务付出多少代价。
运行中的服务持有哪些任务，一条消息怎样经过它们，以及关闭时按什么顺序停下它们。
RustStream 在每条消息上的开销：与各 Broker 裸客户端对照的吞吐量，以及框架自身代码的指令数和内存分配次数。
RustStream 的每个 crate 如何测量自己：三个循环、运行、报告和代码的测量。
每个公布的基准测试数字测的是什么，哪些数字之间可以相互比较。
crate 如何公布基准测试结果：一份放在稳定路径上的 JSON 文档，由基准测试页面读取。
框架自身代码在每条消息上的开销，以指令数和内存分配次数计，以及这些开销花在哪里。
核心不认识任何 Broker：Broker crate 实现核心的 trait，并持有该 Broker 的全部设置。
无法通过编译的错误，以及编译器对每一种错误给出的提示。
Broker 的各个状态都是类型：配置、连接和已关闭的连接；进入每个状态的调用都会消耗前一个状态。
一条消息从 Broker 的流到确认所经过的各个阶段，按运行时执行它们的顺序排列。
一条消息如何确认：处理器返回什么，失败策略如何决定，重试在哪里结束。
RustStream 支持的 Broker：核心自带的内存 Broker，以及每个外部 Broker 各自的 crate，每个 crate 都有自己的文档。
MemoryBroker 是运行在服务进程内的完整 Broker：不需要服务器，由 ruststream 的 memory feature 提供。
The building blocks of a RustStream service, one page per component, grouped by the part of the service they belong to.
A RustStream value names the service, holds its brokers and mounts each handler on the broker it subscribes to.
The attribute turns a builder function into the service's main: a binary that runs the service or prints its AsyncAPI document.
The ruststream command runs a service and prints its AsyncAPI document through cargo run; cargo generate scaffolds a new one.
Four hooks run around the brokers' connection: on_startup, after_startup, on_shutdown and after_shutdown.
A service runs until a signal, until a future of yours, or beside another server that owns the process.
health hands out a HealthProbe that reports whether a started service is running, stopping, stopped or failed, and how many of its subscriptions consume.
An HTTP server owns the process and the service runs beside it: started before the server, stopped after it.
run starts the service and serves until SIGINT or SIGTERM, then shuts it down gracefully.
shutdown stops a started service gracefully: hooks, subscriptions, running handlers, then the brokers.
start brings the service up and returns a RunningApp, so the caller owns the process and decides when it stops.
run_until serves until a future of yours resolves, then shuts the service down gracefully.
Shared state is one value built at startup that every handler reads, as a State<T> parameter or through a dependency-injection container.
on_startup builds one value of any type; a handler takes any of its fields as a State<T> parameter.
froodi is a dependency-injection container whose ruststream feature builds a handler's dependencies per delivery, as Inject parameters.
shaku is a dependency-injection container with no RustStream support; the service builds it in on_startup and a handler resolves from it.
TestApp runs a service's production app in process, drives its brokers and asserts on what its handlers received and published.
How a test publishes to a broker of the app and moves the app forward: settling deliveries and advancing time.
TestApp::advance lets a delay pass, fires the delayed redeliveries now due, and drives their reaction to a standstill.
TestApp::broker_named addresses a broker by the label it was registered under, which tells apart two brokers of one type.
TestApp::broker addresses one broker of the app by its production type, for publishing to it and reading its records.
TestApp::drain waits for the post-settle continuations of everything settled so far, for a test that asserts on their effects.
message(&v) starts an input with the publish builder the service itself publishes through: destination, headers and codec.
TestApp::publish and BrokerHandle::publish send any serde value to a named destination in one call; publish_with_headers adds headers.
publish() sends the input onto the broker and returns once the whole reaction to it has settled, so the next line can assert.
TestApp::settle drives a reaction the test started without the harness to a standstill, without publishing anything new.
TestApp runs a device service's EmbeddedApp on the host: Out slot records, hooks in the test's own future, and a state the test builds.
Hooks run a test's own code at the moment a subscription is called or a message is published.
on_call runs an async closure each time a subscription's handler is called, handing it the subscription's assertions as they stood at that call.
on_publish runs an async closure each time a message is published to a destination, handing it that destination's assertions as they stood at that publish.
Assertions on what was published to one destination: how many messages, their payloads, headers and per-message settings.
assert_called_once checks that exactly one message was published to the destination.
assert_called(n) checks that exactly n messages were published to the destination.
assert_not_called checks that nothing was published to the destination.
assert_options_default checks that the latest recorded publish carried no per-message settings, so the publish policy's defaults applied.
decoded_as::<U>() re-types a record, so its payload assertions decode to U.
decoded returns every payload published to the destination as a value; decoded_with names the codec.
messages returns every message published to the destination, with its name, headers and payload, for checks of your own.
with_header checks one header of the latest message published to the destination, such as one a transform or a publish layer added.
with_options checks the per-message settings the latest recorded publish carried, the value a builder step set.
with_raw checks the bytes of the latest payload published to the destination.
with checks that the latest payload published to the destination decodes to a value; with_codec names the codec.
The records a test reads: what one subscriber received, what was published to a destination, and what went through an Out slot.
TestApp::out opens the record of one Out slot: every message the handler sent through it, on whichever broker it went.
BrokerHandle::published opens the record of one destination on a broker: every message published there, with its name and headers.
BrokerHandle::subscriber opens the record of one subscription: what its handler received and how each delivery settled.
How a test checks whether the app is still running or has shut down, and how its run ended.
TestApp::assert_running asserts the service is still up: no fail-fast failure has shut it down.
TestApp::assert_shut_down asserts a fail-fast failure has shut the service down, as a handler panic does under the default policy.
TestApp::run_result returns what the service run would return now: Ok while it is healthy, an error once a fail-fast failure stopped it.
How a test starts the production app, gives it state, and shuts it down.
TestApp::shutdown tears the service down the way the service does, hooks included, and returns what run would return, so a fail-fast failure fails the test.
start_live connects the brokers of the same app to a running stand, so one test body checks the service against the real broker.
TestApp::start runs the app main builds, unchanged, with every broker connected in process and no server.
TestApp::with_state starts the app with a state the test builds in place of on_startup, wired to the brokers of the app.
Assertions on one subscriber: how often it ran, what it received and how each delivery was settled.
assert_batch_sizes(&[..]) checks how a subscriber's deliveries were cut into handler calls.
assert_called_once checks that a subscriber's handler ran exactly once: one delivery, or one batch.
assert_called(n) checks that a subscriber's handler ran exactly n times, counting a batch as one call.
assert_last_failed_to_decode() checks that the latest delivery did not decode into the handler's input type.
assert_not_called checks that a subscriber's handler never ran.
assert_outcome(..) checks the latest handler call by its classified Outcome, failures included.
batches_raw() returns the bytes a batch handler received, one list per call.
batches::<T>() returns what a batch handler received, one decoded list per call.
outcomes() returns how every handler call settled, in call order.
panicked() checks that the handler panicked on its latest call.
received_raw() returns the bytes of every payload a subscriber received, in delivery order.
received_values::<T>() returns every value a subscriber's deliveries lent its handler, batch elements included.
received::<T>() returns every payload a subscriber received, decoded with the default codec, for a check of your own.
settled(outcome) checks how the latest handler call settled, against the HandlerOutcome a handler returns.
with_raw(bytes) checks the exact bytes of the latest handler call, before any decoding.
with_value(&value) checks the value the latest delivery lent its handler, on a broker whose deliveries already hold one.
with(&value) checks that the latest handler call received this value, decoded with the default codec.
The asyncapi feature generates the AsyncAPI 3.1 document of a service from its app value, with build_spec.
How the document is produced, serialized and served, and where its payload schemas come from.
build_spec reads the AsyncAPI document of a service from its app value, the same value main runs.
asyncapi gen prints the document of a service from the main that #[ruststream::app] generates.
.describe(text) gives a manual registration the operation description the attribute takes from the handler's doc comment.
MessageInfo names the component of a message in the document and describes it, whatever the Rust type is called.
messages_without_schema lists the messages the document describes with no payload schema, for a check to fail on.
A message type that derives JsonSchema gives its message a payload schema in the document.
to_json and to_yaml serialize the document in the two formats AsyncAPI tools read.
.undocumented() takes the schemas of one manual registration out of the document and lifts its JsonSchema demand.
render_viewer_html returns a self-contained HTML page that renders the document with the AsyncAPI React component.
What the document says about a service beyond its channels: replies, channel parameters, headers, content types and retries.
A destination declared as a name template becomes a channel whose address keeps its placeholders, each one declared as a parameter.
Each message names the media type of the codec that reads or writes it; the root defaultContentType appears only when all of them agree.
A header contract becomes the headers schema of its message, from a Headers<T> parameter or from #[outgoing(headers = ..)].
A subscription over an InMessages set lists one message per variant, each with its own name, description, headers and content type.
A reply is the reply of the receive operation it answers: the document names its channel and its message.
The attempt cap and the dead-letter destination of a registration appear on its receive operation as the x-ruststream-retry extension.
The servers section: the brokers a service connects to, how clients authenticate, and the protocol bindings.
Bindings carry what one protocol says about a server, a channel, an operation or a message, in that protocol's AsyncAPI vocabulary.
ServerSpec::security attaches a SecurityScheme that says how clients authenticate; each scheme becomes a component the server references.
RustStream::server declares a server the document lists, from a ServerSpec that says how clients reach the broker.
with_broker_labeled registers a broker under a label that is its server name in the document, and the broker describes the server.
The info section: what the service is, who owns it and under which license.
AppId is the identifier of the service at the root of the document, a URI parsed when it is built.
AppInfo is the info section of the document: the title and the version, a description and the terms of service.
Contact names who answers for the service: a person or a team, a URL and an e-mail address, each optional.
ExternalDocs points at documentation kept outside the document: a URL and what the reader finds there.
License names the license the service is published under, with an optional URL of its text.
A Tag is a label that groups the service among its neighbours, with an optional description and link.
MemoryBroker is a complete broker inside the service's process, and the reference implementation of the broker contract.
A MemoryPattern subscription reads every name its pattern matches, and the broker's Routing decides who receives a shared match.
A retaining MemoryBroker keeps the newest messages of every name within a bound, and its subscriptions replay over them.
Logs, metrics and traces of a running service: each comes from a layer on the app and a feature that exports it.
The logging feature prints the service's tracing events on the console, colored, at the verbosity RUST_LOG sets.
The metrics feature counts and times deliveries and counts publishes in a Prometheus registry that the service serves on /metrics.
Otel sends the service's spans and metrics to an OpenTelemetry collector over OTLP, the dispatch metrics included.
The otel feature carries the W3C trace context from a delivery to its replies and opens a span for every delivery.
TracingLayer logs every delivery and its outcome as tracing events, so handlers hold no logging code of their own.
#[subscriber] turns an async fn over a reference to the message into a handler that include mounts on a broker.
A handler over &[T] runs once per batch the broker delivers; the mount site names the batch size, and the body settles the batch or each element.
A codec turns a payload into a message type and back; it is a compile-time type, chosen at the mount site, and JSON is the default.
A handler that reads the delivery's bytes as they arrived, and a reply that leaves as the bytes it holds, skip the codec.
CborCodec reads and writes CBOR through ciborium, a compact binary format with the data model of JSON; it is on with the cbor feature.
A codec of your own implements the Codec trait over any serde format and mounts wherever a built-in codec does.
JsonCodec reads and writes JSON through serde_json; it is the default codec, on with the json feature.
MsgpackCodec reads and writes MessagePack through rmp-serde; a struct travels as an array of its field values. It is on with the msgpack feature.
A message generated by prost carries its own bytes with #[wire(prost)]: no serde, no codec feature, encoded once into the buffer that leaves.
A handler's parameters after the message: the per-delivery Context and the values extracted from it.
Ctx<K> passes one field of the broker's per-delivery context to the handler as a parameter.
Context carries one delivery's channel, headers, state and broker fields to the middleware and the handler.
A type that implements FromContext becomes a handler parameter, resolved from the delivery before the body runs.
How many deliveries of one subscription run at once, and on which threads.
The poll-diagnostics feature times the polls of every handler and names the handlers that compute on the app's runtime.
threads(n) gives a subscription n threads of its own, so a handler that computes leaves the app's runtime free for I/O.
workers(n) handles up to n deliveries of one subscription at once; workers(n, by_key) keeps the deliveries of one key in order.
What a subscriber does when its handler panics or a payload cannot decode, set per subscriber with on_failure.
An enum deriving InMessages declares several message types on one subscription: a rule picks the variant, and the document lists one message per variant.
What a handler returns settles its delivery: ack, retry, retry after a delay, or drop, as a HandlerOutcome.
and_after attaches a continuation to an outcome: work that runs on a task of its own once the delivery is settled.
What the handler body returns settles the delivery: a HandlerOutcome, nothing at all, or a Result.
A post-settle hook registered on the context runs once the delivery is settled, only for the settlement it names.
retry_after(delay) asks for the delivery back no sooner than the delay, for a condition that will pass.
Layers wrap handlers and publishes: app-wide, per router or per registration.
A DynStack is a handler middleware chain assembled when the app starts, mounted on one registration as one layer.
A layer wraps handlers in code of your own: every handler of the app, every handler of a router, or one registration.
A PublishDynStack is a publish middleware chain assembled when the app starts, added to the app as one publish layer.
A publish layer wraps every message the app's handlers publish: it changes the message, observes the send, or refuses it.
Settings the attribute leaves open are chained where the handler is mounted: name, workers, failure policy, batch size and start position.
How a handler answers a message and publishes to other destinations.
A handler consumes from one broker and publishes through another, named by a token the target broker mints before registration.
An Out slot hands a handler a live publisher as a parameter: one marker per slot, bound to a publish policy at the mount site.
A message type declares where it goes: a fixed name, a name template with a setter per placeholder, or no name, left to the call.
One builder publishes every message: message(&value), the positions its type leaves open, then publish().
A broker's per-message settings, such as a priority, a QoS or a key: defaulted by the publish policy, set per publish by the broker's own steps.
The publisher capabilities a broker offers, one trait each, starting with Publisher.
OwnedTransactions opens independent transactions that own their buffers, so a handler keeps several open on one slot at once.
Publisher is the capability every slot names; a publish policy at the mount site becomes one when startup pairs it with the connected broker.
RequestReply sends a request from a handler and awaits the correlated answer, on a broker that correlates replies natively.
TransactionalPublisher puts several publishes in one broker transaction: every reply of a batch, or a scope a handler opens on its slot.
A handler answers a message by returning a value; the reply type or the mount site says where the answer goes.
A publish transform changes an outgoing message at one publish position, before it reaches the publisher.
A batch publish transform is a step on the replies of a batch handler: each reply passes it on its own, with the batch's context.
A naming transform sets the destination of each message, on a position where nothing else declared it: a reply to the inbox a request named.
A publish transform is a static step on one publish position: it reads the delivery or the slot, and changes the outgoing message.
A subscription over a replayable log opens at a position of your choice, and its handler can move it.
A handler moves its own subscription to another position of the log through the broker's seek handle.
start_at opens a replayable subscription at a position: the start of the log, a sequence number, or the tip.
max_attempts(n) ends a message that keeps coming back, and dead_letter(name) is where it goes then.
The Retry slot is the publisher a copy of a delivery leaves through; out_retry replaces it and to(name) names its destination.
A Router groups one module's handlers with their own middleware and codec, and include_router mounts the group on a broker.
A [subscriber](./index.md) reads a subscription named by a string or by the broker's descriptor, fixed in the attribute or left to the mount site.
A serde struct is the header contract a handler reads and a publish writes, checked in both directions.
insert_typed writes a header contract into a header map, the way a publish transform stamps every message of a slot.
Message<H, T> hands a handler the decoded payload and its parsed header contract as one input.
A message type names its header contract, so publishing it does not compile without the headers.
指南带你从一个空 crate 走到一个运行中的 RustStream 服务。
十一章内容逐步扩展同一个 RustStream 服务（一家小商店），从第一个订阅者一直到联网的 Broker。
asyncapi gen 打印商店的 AsyncAPI 文档：每个主题、谁读谁写、schema、重试上限，以及应用对自己的描述。
打包是计算任务，所以它有两个专属线程；预约快递要等待网络，所以四个预约同时进行。
店面通过 HTTP 接收订单，把订单连同事件一起存储；中继把事件交给 Broker，商店运行在服务器旁边。
documents.s: 在 HTTP 服务器旁运行，outbox

documents.t: 订单扩展为带订单行的载荷，加上每次发布都必须携带的消息头契约，以及按主题选定的编解码器。
documents.s: 消息：载荷、消息头、编解码器

documents.t: 应用用两层包裹每个订阅者：一层记录每次投递及其结果，另一层是商店自己的，对运行过慢的处理器发出警告。
更换构建商店所用的 Broker，商店就迁移到 NATS；订阅者和路由器的设置都保持不变。
accept 用一个支付请求回复每个订单，并通过 Out 槽位通知顾客。路由器决定两者如何发出。
documents.s: 回复与发布到其他主题

documents.t: 商店从一个订阅者起步。它接收每一个已下的订单，由一个小应用挂载在内存 Broker 上。
documents.s: 服务和它的第一个订阅者

documents.t: 支付服务商每次拒绝，charge 都给出所需的结果：立即重试、稍后重试、丢弃，或者转入死信主题。
支付客户端和邮件发送器在启动时打开一次，以 State 的形式到达每个订阅者；上下文告诉订阅者它拿到的是哪次投递。

documents.t: 本节介绍 RustStream 是如何构建的，以及它的设计让服务付出多少代价。

一条消息的各个步骤，放在执行该步骤的任务那一列循环任务处理任务稍后，受跟踪下一轮启动轮询流构建上下文消费层解码处理器函数体发布应答确认轮询下一条后续任务与定时器 以文字阅读本图 循环任务: 轮询 流; 轮询 下一条 处理任务: 构建 上下文; 消费层; 解码; 处理器 函数体; 发布 应答; 确认 稍后，受跟踪: 后续任务 与定时器 轮询 流 → 构建 上下文 构建 上下文 → 消费层 消费层 → 解码 解码 → 处理器 函数体 处理器 函数体 → 发布 应答 发布 应答 → 确认 确认 → 轮询 下一条: 下一轮 确认 → 后续任务 与定时器: 启动 默认情况下，处理任务就是循环任务本身；使用 workers(n) 时是一个 worker 任务；使用 threads(n) 时是一个专用线程。and_after 后续任务、确认之后的钩子和 retry_after 定时器在确认之后启动，作为应用跟踪的任务运行。它们最多执行一次：此时消息已经确认。

优雅关闭依次做了什么信号、fail-fast或 RunningApp::shutdown运行 on_shutdown 钩子，此时 Broker 仍在连接各循环不再接收新消息手上的消息处理完并确认受跟踪的后续任务和重试定时器执行完Broker 按注册的相反顺序关闭运行 after_shutdown 钩子，此时 Broker 已关闭 以文字阅读本图 信号、fail-fast 或 RunningApp::shutdown → 运行 on_shutdown 钩子， 此时 Broker 仍在连接 运行 on_shutdown 钩子， 此时 Broker 仍在连接 → 各循环不再 接收新消息 各循环不再 接收新消息 → 手上的消息 处理完并确认 手上的消息 处理完并确认 → 受跟踪的后续任务 和重试定时器执行完 受跟踪的后续任务 和重试定时器执行完 → Broker 按注册的 相反顺序关闭 Broker 按注册的 相反顺序关闭 → 运行 after_shutdown 钩子， 此时 Broker 已关闭 关闭超时限制等待的时长。超时之后，仍在运行的循环会被中止，尚未完成的受跟踪任务则任其自行结束。不设超时时，关闭会等待全部任务完成。在专用线程上用普通 tokio::spawn 启动的任务不受跟踪，随线程一起结束。

RustStream 在每条消息上的开销：一是与各 Broker 裸客户端的对照，二是框架自身代码的开销。 Broker 客户端和你的处理器之间隔着一层框架，每条消息都要为它花时间：订阅流、解码、分发、ack。 本页把这份代价公布两次，用两种测量回答两个不同的问题。 第一种是在真实 Broker 上、与裸客户端对照的吞吐量，同一台机器，同样的工作。它说明已部署的服务 付出了多少。 第二种是代码本身的开销：每条消息的指令数和内存分配次数。在 ruststream 里，这是框架自身代码的 开销，数字里不含 Broker。它说明代码变动之后有什么变了，而且足够精确，可以让一个把消息变贵的 pull request 通不过。 每个 crate 按同一套方法论测量自己，并公布自己的数字。 本页从各 crate 仓库的 main 分支读取这些数字，每个 crate 占一个标签页。新的测量结果一经合并， 就会出现在它的标签页里。这些数字能说明什么、不能说明什么，见数字。

Broker 标签页里的第一张图是对照图。每个场景画出三个循环，每个循环跑三个交替轮次，坐标轴的零点是裸客户端的最佳一轮。一个循环画成 一条横条，从最佳一轮延伸到最慢的一轮；圆点标出最佳一轮，缺口标出中位一轮。圆点在零点右侧， 表示比裸客户端慢。最佳的一轮最接近未受干扰的开销，中位的一轮则是重跑一次通常会得到的那一轮。 零点周围的阴影带是 RustStream 的 无法区分 判定的依据：最佳一轮到最差一轮之间的波动范围。 最佳一轮落在带内，就与裸客户端无法区分。空心圆点标出 crate 判定为无法区分的循环，每行旁边的 判定由该 crate 自己公布。鼠标悬停或键盘聚焦时，该行 显示自己的数字；图表下方的表格列出全部数字：最佳一轮，括号里是中位数。 “Broker crate”是该 crate 自己的消费者和发布者，不带运行时，因此两项差值可以分开读：crate 比 客户端多付多少，运行时又在其上多付多少。 如果 crate 还提供插件，插件的场景画在单独的一张图上，用自己的坐标轴。图中的三个循环是同一个应用的 三种写法：不用插件、手写插件、使用 crate 自带的插件。插件的表格和 crate 自带插件旁边的判定，还给出它比手写插件多付出多少。

代码开销图是每个标签页的最后一张图，也是核心标签页唯一的一张图。它展示稳态下每条消息的指令数和内存分配次数。这些是绝对数值，不是对照：框架相对于 Broker 客户端 多付出多少，看对照图。ruststream 在进程内传输上测量框架自身的代码。Broker crate 在真实的传输上测量自己，数字里包含什么，写在它的基准测试页面上。 每个 crate 各用一条坐标轴，因为 Broker crate 的数字里还包含它的客户端的工作。“冷启动”是启动 服务并处理第一条消息一共花掉的指令数和内存分配次数；这笔开销一个服务只付一次，不按消息计。 鼠标悬停或聚焦时该行会显示它，图表下方的表格也列出它。每个 crate 图表上方那一行先写跑出这些数字的机器，一直写到内存，再写这次测量的 crate 版本、ruststream 版本和测量日期。只有知道两台机器上编译的是同一份代码，指令数才能互相比较。

RustStream 的每个 crate 如何测量自己，使一个 Broker 公布的数字与另一个 Broker 的含义相同。 每个 Broker crate 都遵循下面的流程。这样一来，不同 Broker 公布的数字含义相同。偏离流程的 Broker 会在自己的页面上说明。

一次运行把同一个场景测三遍，三者只有一个区别：消息由什么承载。 裸客户端。 Broker 自己的客户端，直接驱动。 Broker crate。 该 crate 自己的消费者和发布者（它的订阅描述符、它产出的订阅者流、它的 确认、它的发布者）由基准测试里的一个循环驱动，上面没有运行时。 RustStream。 用户写的那整个服务：处理器、应用、分发。 第一项差值是这个 Broker crate 比它所包装的客户端多付出多少，这由 crate 自己负责。第二项是 运行时在其上多付出多少，而且是在这个 Broker 上；它按 Broker 分别公布，因为各个 crate 与运行时 相接的方式不同：流如何产出、投递是否成批到达、背压如何传到消费者。 同一个客户端，同一套客户端配置。 预取、ack 模式、consumer group、持久化、连接数和 Broker 特有的调优，三个循环完全一致。框架一侧通过 RustStream 配置 Broker，最终生成的客户端设置 仍然必须相同。 ack 的位置相同。 RustStream 在处理器返回之后 ack，因此另外两个循环也在同一位置 ack。在裸运行 的末尾批量 ack，测的是另一种协议，而不是另一个框架。 解码成同一个类型。 没有处理器的那两个循环用同样的编解码器把载荷反序列化成同一个结构体，并通过 std::hint::black_box 访问其中一个字段。省掉这一步，最容易得出错误的数字：解码结果没有人 用，优化器就会把解码删掉，裸的一侧于是悄悄不再解码。 载荷逐字节相同。 每个循环消费的消息体都来自同一个生成器。 运行时相同。 tokio 的 flavor、工作线程数和同时在处理的消息条数，在三个循环里都一样。 构建相同。 构建配置、RUSTFLAGS 和分配器一致，可观测性 feature（logging、metrics、 otel）要么每个循环都关，要么每个循环都开。环境里带着 -C target-cpu=native 的机器，产出的数字 别的机器复现不了，因此这些标志与结果一起公布。

消费者在第一条消息发布之前就已连接。 否则一侧消费的是 Broker 里已有的积压，另一侧收到 的是实时投递，而在多数 Broker 里这是两条不同的路径。 每次运行都用自己的名字。 subject、队列、流或 consumer group 每次运行都新建，这样第 N 次 运行绝不会看到第 N-1 次留下的东西。 计时窗口从收到第一条消息开始，到最后一条完成 ack 结束。 测量的运行之前，先跑一次校准 运行并丢弃结果。建立连接、注册消费者和最初的内存分配属于启动开销，不属于每条消息的开销。 消息条数要让一次运行至少持续五秒，这样启动阶段的瞬态和计时器精度都落在噪声范围内。 各个循环是交替的，不是分块的。 裸、crate、框架，裸、crate、框架，如此往复，共三轮。先把 一个循环整个跑完再跑下一个，会把机器的全部漂移（发热、后台负载、页缓存）算到最后跑的那个 循环头上。

每个循环都报告三轮：最佳、中位和最差。 机器上的噪声只会让运行变慢，所以最快的一轮最接近 未受干扰的开销，中位的一轮是典型的一轮，最慢的一轮则说明机器离安静有多远。单次运行的单个 数字不算结果。 表格里印出最佳的一轮，括号里是中位数。 最差的一轮留在文档里，不进入单元格：它的用处是 波动范围，也就是最佳的一轮到最差的一轮之间的距离。 小于该波动范围的差异公布为 无法区分， 而不是一个百分比：低于运行间噪声的数值，读起来 像是从未测到过的精度。 饱和的消费者要标注出来。 当裸的一侧整个运行都在等 Broker 时，该行带上 broker-bound。 环境与数字一起公布：CPU 型号与核心数、内核、Broker 如何启动（镜像、容器、主机）、rustc 版本、各 crate 版本、构建配置和编译标志。没有这些，一个数字既无法复现，也无法判断它是否过时。

每个 crate 都用自己的基准测试命令，生成它的代码开销图。 命令名写在该 crate 的基准测试页面上，在 ruststream 里是 just bench。这条命令需要 valgrind， 以及与该 crate 所依赖版本一致的基准测试 runner。 在 ruststream 里，just bench 5000 让每个场景在五千次投递上测量，而不是一千次：数字更稳， 运行更久；发布的文档仍按默认值测量。 每个场景都是用户写的那个服务，由真实运行时启动，测试用的 harness 不参与编译，测的因此 就是发布出去的代码。数字是绝对值；在 ruststream 里，它就是框架自身的开销。与别人写的 客户端相比，是对照图的事，由 Broker crate 来做。 ruststream 的传输是进程内的。 被测的是框架自身的代码，数字不应随套接字、服务器负载或 网络而变。Broker crate 在真实的传输上测量，这给数字带来了什么，写在它的基准测试页面上。 队列在测量区间打开之前就已填满。 场景测的是稳态投递，不含连接、订阅建立，以及它们背后的 首批内存分配。 采集只覆盖测量区间，不越界。 准备和收尾跑在同一个进程里，走的是同一份框架代码，把它们也 算进去的测量，会把填满队列的开销当成清空队列的开销报出来。 每个场景跑三次，各有各的用处。 一条消息，再加两次更长的运行，后一次的投递数是前一次的 两倍：在 ruststream 里是一千条和两千条，Broker crate 的条数写在它的基准测试页面上。 后两次之差是服务跑起来之后一条消息的开销，只投递一条的那次就是冷启动。运行途中不需要关掉 任何东西，正是这一点让这个办法对内存分配计数器也成立，因为它根本没有开关。 每个场景两个数字。 callgrind 给出的指令数是精确的，用来对照；DHAT 给出的内存分配次数是 精确的，由场景声明的下限把住。在 ruststream 里，另有一个基准程序用自己的场景测量时钟时间。 这些时间有噪声，just bench 把它们打印出来，仅供参考。 是对照，不是门槛。 带上 --baseline=main 运行时，基准测试命令把一个分支与目标分支上 同一套基准测试的结果对照：某个场景的指令数增幅超过该 crate 自己的上限，就算失败。 ruststream 的上限是两个百分点，Broker crate 的上限写在它的基准测试页面上。 上限是相对的，所以只在与基线对照时生效。 超出场景声明的内存分配次数，则不论有没有基线都算失败。 pull request 的作者自己运行对照并引用它的数字，而降低了某个场景的改动， 也在同一个 pull request 里降低它声明的下限。冷启动也按同样的规则检查。
每个公布的数字测的是什么，哪些数字之间可以相互比较。

每一行都由维护该 Broker crate 的人测出，在自己的机器上，对着 localhost 上的 Broker。 因此行与行之间不可比：一行的绝对吞吐量说明不了另一行的任何事情。可比的只有同一行里的各个循环， 结果要做的正是这一比较。 localhost 上的 Broker，对框架来说是最苛刻的环境。这里没有网络延迟。每条消息的绝对开销不变， 因此占的比例比隔着真实网络时更大。应把该百分比读作已部署服务所付代价的上界，而不是典型值。 “受 Broker 限制”标记表示，裸客户端在整个运行的大部分时间里都在等套接字。框架的工作于是发生在 原本就在等待的时间里，测出的差异趋近于零。对这类负载来说这是真实结果：饱和的消费者就是这样。 但这样的数字是分发开销的下界，不是对它的测量，切勿读成“免费”。

指令数是精确的。在 ruststream 里，同一个二进制程序跑两次得到同一个数字，快一倍的机器也得到 同一个数字，因此 ruststream 的各行之间可比，与另一台机器上测出的同一行也可比。指令数说明不了 的是时间：同样的指令数，在缓存未命中处要花更多时间。 在 ruststream 里，这个数字就是本 crate 自身的工作，此外别无他物： 用户写的服务，跑在进程内队列上，把载荷解码成一个类型、读一个字段、确认投递。里面没有 Broker， 所以只有框架的代码变了，数字才会变。这正是两个百分点可以算作缺陷而不是噪声的原因。 每条消息的数字都是稳态。启动服务的开销只付一次：连接、建立订阅，以及它们背后的首批内存分配。 把它摊到一次运行的消息上，等于把一次性的价钱当成每条消息的价钱公布出去。因此每个场景测两次， 第二次的投递数是第一次的两倍，一条消息的开销就是两次运行之差；冷启动单独测，只投递一条消息。 在 ruststream 里，这两次分别是一千条和两千条。 内存分配按每条消息统计。在 ruststream 里，投递路径上是零：服务跑起来之后，消息从队列走到 处理器函数体，框架一次也没有向分配器要过内存。ruststream 发布路径上的数字，就是 Broker 为持有交给它的消息所要的那几次分配，此外再无其他。 Broker crate 在真实的传输上测量自己，多数是对着自己 compose 文件里的 Broker。因此它的数字里 还包含客户端的工作，每次运行之间也会有少许变动。数字包含哪些开销、变动多大、两次运行各投递 多少条、受哪个上限约束，都写在该 crate 的基准测试页面上。
crate 如何公布基准测试结果：一份放在稳定路径上的 JSON 文档，由基准测试页面读取。 Broker crate 用 just bench 对着自己 compose 文件里的 Broker 运行自己的基准程序。它把结果 提交到自己的仓库：一个供人阅读的页面，和一份供基准测试页面读取的 JSON 文档。
该文件位于 Broker 仓库的 docs/benchmarks/results.json，紧挨着解释它的页面。基准测试页面从 main 分支读取它，所以新的测量结果合并后立即可见。 https://raw.githubusercontent.com/powersemmi/<crate>/main/docs/benchmarks/results.json

接收一条消息不做任何内存分配。循环为消息保留一个槽位和一个编码缓冲区，每个阶段都是在编译期确定的泛型类型，途中没有动态调用。在运行时组装的 DynStack 每层每条消息花费一个装箱的 future。and_after 后续任务是一个装箱的 future，只有设置了它的消息才需要付出。 如果 Broker 客户端只读取字节，应答不做任何内存分配：它借用循环的缓冲区。进程内 Broker 会保留交给它的内容，所以它的应答要付出编解码器写入的那块缓冲区。其余发布场景分配的，是进程内 Broker 为每条消息保留的内容，以及场景自己构建的东西：一个消息头的值，或一个请求的一次性收件箱。 解码中最贵的是消息内容的大小：对比 1 KB 的消息体和小结构体。基准测试公布了每个场景及其方法，也包括与各 Broker 裸客户端的对照。

核心不认识任何 Broker：Broker crate 实现核心的 trait，并持有该 Broker 的全部设置。 服务、与 Broker 无关的核心，以及实现核心 trait 的 Broker crate挂载到实现实现封装封装你的服务ruststreamBroker crate#[subscriber]处理器#[ruststream::app]构建函数运行时：路由、分发、确认、发布编解码器：JSON、CBOR、MessagePack 或不用，在编译期选定特性：内存 Broker、AsyncAPI、指标、OpenTelemetry、测试Broker, Subscriber,Publisher, sources,policies能力：批量、事务、请求与应答、定位读取ruststream-natssubject、stream、策略、设置、挂载步骤ruststream-rdkafkatopic、消费组、策略、设置、挂载步骤async-natsrdkafka 以文字阅读本图 你的服务: #[subscriber] 处理器; #[ruststream::app] 构建函数 ruststream: 运行时：路由、分发、 确认、发布; 编解码器：JSON、CBOR、 MessagePack 或不用， 在编译期选定; 特性：内存 Broker、 AsyncAPI、指标、 OpenTelemetry、测试; Broker, Subscriber, Publisher, sources, policies; 能力：批量、事务、 请求与应答、 定位读取 Broker crate: ruststream-nats subject、stream、 策略、设置、 挂载步骤; ruststream-rdkafka topic、消费组、 策略、设置、 挂载步骤 #[subscriber] 处理器 → 运行时：路由、分发、 确认、发布: 挂载到 ruststream-nats subject、stream、 策略、设置、 挂载步骤 → Broker, Subscriber, Publisher, sources, policies: 实现 ruststream-rdkafka topic、消费组、 策略、设置、 挂载步骤 → 能力：批量、事务、 请求与应答、 定位读取: 实现 ruststream-nats subject、stream、 策略、设置、 挂载步骤 → async-nats: 封装 ruststream-rdkafka topic、消费组、 策略、设置、 挂载步骤 → rdkafka: 封装 核心不依赖任何 Broker 客户端。必需的 trait 只有三个：连接的生命周期、以 Stream 形式交付消息的订阅者，以及发布者。批量、事务、请求与应答、定位读取，以及消息本身已携带的值，都是能力 trait；只有客户端支持时，Broker 才实现它们。 Broker 的专有概念都在它自己的 crate 里：订阅形式的描述符、发布者的策略、单条消息的设置，以及读取挂载链设置的挂载步骤。核心里没有任何 Broker 专属的设置，也没有它们的默认值。 编解码器是一个类型：挂载时指定的编解码器，或由启用的特性选出的默认编解码器。没有启用任何编解码器特性时就没有默认值，需要编解码器的挂载无法通过编译。 trait、运行时和每个可选层都是独立的 crate，ruststream 在同一套路径下重新导出它们。分层由编译器保证：契约 crate ruststream-core 不依赖框架中的任何其他 crate。它以 #![no_std] 构建，只需要内存分配器，因此设备也可以依赖它；ruststream 会在每个带操作系统的目标平台上打开它的 std 特性。投递主体（解码、中间件、处理器、回复、确认）位于 ruststream-runtime，它不绑定任何执行器，而是对运行时的时钟和应用停止的等待保持泛型。ruststream-runtime-tokio 在 tokio 上运行它，并负责属于 tokio 的部分：应用的生命周期、任务派生、工作池、专用线程和信号。服务代码需要等待时调用 ruststream::time::sleep，它按应用的时钟睡眠，因此测试工具会和其他计时器一起推进它。ruststream 的 cargo 特性打开一个可选层：内存 Broker、AsyncAPI、指标、日志、OpenTelemetry、测试和命令行。特性只会增加功能，不会改变其他特性的行为。

Broker 的各个状态都是类型：配置、连接和已关闭的连接；进入每个状态的调用都会消耗前一个状态。 Broker 的状态作为类型，以及让它从一个状态进入下一个状态的应用步骤connect(self)shutdown(self)start()shutdown()Broker应用B::new(config)同步，无 I/OB::Connectedsubscribe, publishClosed关闭报告构建函数注册 Broker和处理器RunningApp已连接，循环在运行已停止循环已排空，Broker 已关闭比 Broker 连接活得更久的发布者会返回错误，而不是默默成功 以文字阅读本图 Broker: B::new(config) 同步，无 I/O; B::Connected subscribe, publish; Closed 关闭报告 应用: 构建函数 注册 Broker 和处理器; RunningApp 已连接， 循环在运行; 已停止 循环已排空， Broker 已关闭 B::new(config) 同步，无 I/O → B::Connected subscribe, publish: connect(self) B::Connected subscribe, publish → Closed 关闭报告: shutdown(self) 构建函数 注册 Broker 和处理器 → RunningApp 已连接， 循环在运行: start() RunningApp 已连接， 循环在运行 → 已停止 循环已排空， Broker 已关闭: shutdown() 比 Broker 连接活得更久的发布者 会返回错误，而不是默默成功 创建 Broker 不做任何 I/O，所以无论用哪个 Broker，#[ruststream::app] 的构建函数都保持同步。所有网络调用都等到 start() 才发生。 订阅和发布只是已连接形式的方法。在 connect 之前持有 Broker 的代码没有可用来订阅的东西，而 shutdown 会消耗它关闭的连接，所以这类错误无法通过编译。 start() 按注册顺序连接 Broker，在各自已连接的 Broker 上打开每个订阅，然后运行 after_startup 钩子。途中任何一步失败，已经打开的部分会按相反顺序关闭。shutdown() 停下各循环，等它们排空，再按注册的相反顺序关闭 Broker。每个钩子在哪一步运行，画在异步一页上。 早先交出去的发布者可能比连接活得更久。关闭之后再用它会返回错误。一致性测试套件要求每个 Broker crate 都遵守这条规则。

处理器、路由器、编解码器和中间件都不依赖 Broker。把服务换到另一个 Broker，你只需要改 with_broker 里的一行。 框架自带一个完整的内存 Broker，用于单个应用内部的队列。基于外部服务的 Broker 是独立的 crate，加进 依赖即可使用。 每个 Broker crate 都有自己的文档站点，链接在下表的“文档”列和 Broker 菜单里。 Broker Crate 传输 文档 内存 ruststream（feature memory） 进程内队列，无需外部服务 本站 NATS ruststream-nats Core NATS 与 JetStream powersemmi.github.io/ruststream-nats Redis ruststream-fred Redis Streams（单机、集群、哨兵） powersemmi.github.io/ruststream-fred RabbitMQ ruststream-lapin AMQP 0.9.1（队列、交换机、发布者确认、direct reply-to） powersemmi.github.io/ruststream-lapin Kafka ruststream-rdkafka Apache Kafka（消费者组、提交跟踪、事务、精确一次管道） powersemmi.github.io/ruststream-rdkafka AMQP 1.0 ruststream-amqp ActiveMQ Artemis、RabbitMQ 4.x、Azure Service Bus，以及更广泛的 AMQP 1.0 家族（请求-响应、事务） powersemmi.github.io/ruststream-amqp Google Cloud Pub/Sub ruststream-gcp-pubsub 基于官方客户端的 Pub/Sub（排序键、精确一次确认、死信策略） powersemmi.github.io/ruststream-gcp-pubsub AWS SQS / SNS ruststream-sqs-sns SQS 队列配合 SNS 扇出（FIFO 组、可见性管理、原生的延迟重试） powersemmi.github.io/ruststream-sqs-sns Apache Pulsar ruststream-pulsar Pulsar 主题与主题模式（订阅模式、死信策略、重新定位） powersemmi.github.io/ruststream-pulsar MQTT 5 ruststream-rumqttc MQTT v5（QoS 等级、共享组、保留消息） powersemmi.github.io/ruststream-rumqttc ZeroMQ ruststream-zeromq 无 Broker 的 PUSH/PULL、PUB/SUB，以及基于 TCP 和 IPC 的 DEALER/ROUTER 请求-响应 powersemmi.github.io/ruststream-zeromq 流文件 / stdio ruststream-sea-file 持久、可重放的流文件与 shell 管道；零基础设施，支持完整的重新定位 powersemmi.github.io/ruststream-sea-file AWS Kinesis ruststream-kinesis Kinesis 数据流（分片租约、检查点、重新定位） powersemmi.github.io/ruststream-kinesis SQL 数据库 ruststream-sqlx 服务自有的 Postgres、MySQL/MariaDB 和 SQLite 表中的任务队列，以及基于任意 Broker 的事务性 outbox；SQL 语句在启动时或编译时检查 powersemmi.github.io/ruststream-sqlx 要为别的传输实现 Broker，从 Broker trait 的文档读起：其中写明了 Broker crate 要实现的契约，以及检查该契约的一致性测试套件。

每个 Broker 都是同步构造的，运行时在应用启动时连接它。下面的例子里，只有构造 Broker 的那一行不同。 内存 NATS Redis RabbitMQ Kafka use ruststream::memory::MemoryBroker; use ruststream::runtime::{AppInfo, RustStream}; #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| b.include_router(routes::orders())) } use ruststream::runtime::{AppInfo, RustStream}; use ruststream_nats::NatsBroker; #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(NatsBroker::new("nats://localhost:4222"), |b| { b.include_router(routes::orders()) }) } use ruststream::runtime::{AppInfo, RustStream}; use ruststream_fred::RedisBroker; #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(RedisBroker::standalone("redis://localhost:6379"), |b| { b.include_router(routes::orders()) }) } use ruststream::runtime::{AppInfo, RustStream}; use ruststream_lapin::LapinBroker; #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(LapinBroker::new("amqp://localhost:5672"), |b| { b.include_router(routes::orders()) }) } use ruststream::runtime::{AppInfo, RustStream}; use ruststream_rdkafka::KafkaBroker; #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .with_broker( KafkaBroker::new(["localhost:9092"]).default_group("orders"), |b| { b.include_router(routes::orders()) }, ) } 每个 Broker crate 在自己的文档里说明连接选项。订阅需要 Broker 专有的选项时（消费者组、 durable 名称），你可以在 #[subscriber(..)] 属性里给出该 Broker 的描述符；参见 Broker 专有的描述符。

MemoryBroker 是一个运行在服务进程内部的完整 Broker。它属于 ruststream 的 memory feature， 不需要服务器，适合只属于单个应用的队列。默认的 cargo generate 模板就以它起步。 ruststream = { version = "0.8", features = ["macros", "memory", "json"] } 用法见 Memory broker 组件：Broker 本身及其 prelude、可供重放的 保留日志，以及按模式订阅。
The building blocks of a RustStream service, one page per component, grouped by the part of the service they belong to.

A RustStream value names the service, holds its brokers and mounts each handler on the broker it subscribes to. AppInfo holds the service's title and version, and AppInfo::new takes them. They name the service in its logs and in its AsyncAPI document. with_broker registers one broker, hands its closure a BrokerScope, and mounts the chain the closure returns: |b| b.include(accept).include(audit). Each handler is one more .include(..) on that chain, after the steps of the one before it. A broker the service only publishes to returns the empty chain, |b| b. A service with several brokers calls it once per broker. A broker constructor does no I/O: the application connects every broker when it starts. Handlers mounted with b.include(..) decode with the default codec; with_broker_codec names another one for the whole scope. register_broker adds a broker that only publishes, with no label and no handlers. A builder function returns impl App, so its signature stays the same as layers and state are added.

Macros Manual examples/quickstart.rs #[derive(Debug, Deserialize)] struct Order { id: u64, } #[subscriber("orders")] async fn handle(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "got order"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/quickstart.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| b.include(handle)) } examples/manual/quickstart.rs #[derive(Debug, Deserialize, schemars::JsonSchema)] struct Order { id: u64, } /// The handler: `#[subscriber("orders")]` generates this type and this impl. Every axis of the /// form - the reply, the injections, the broker context, the application state - is a defaulted /// parameter of `Handle`, so a plain body names none of them. struct Receive; impl Handle<Order> for Receive { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "got order"); ready(Ok(())) } } examples/manual/quickstart.rs fn app() -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Receive).build()) }) } fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) }

The #[ruststream::app] attribute turns a builder function into the service's main: a binary that runs the service or prints its AsyncAPI document. The attribute keeps the function and adds a main that hands it to run_main. The function is synchronous, takes no arguments and returns impl App or a RustStream; any other signature is a compile error. The function is the application builder, unchanged. The binary reads its first argument as a command, the same commands the CLI drives through cargo run. run, or no argument, runs the service until SIGINT or SIGTERM. asyncapi gen prints the AsyncAPI document; -o <file> writes it to a file and --yaml switches the format from JSON. asyncapi gen needs the crate's asyncapi feature. With the logging feature, run installs the console logger first, unless the service installed a subscriber of its own. An error is printed to stderr and the process exits with a failure code. The attribute takes the runtime arguments of #[tokio::main]: flavor = "current_thread" and worker_threads = n. The default is a multi-threaded runtime with one worker per core. A hand-written main calls run_main_on to choose the runtime as an AppRuntime value. A test runs the same builder function on TestApp, as the example does.

Macros Manual examples/app_macro.rs #[subscriber("orders")] async fn accept(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "accepted"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| b.include(accept)) } examples/manual/app_macro.rs struct Accept; impl Handle<Order> for Accept { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "accepted"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Accept).build()) }) } // What `#[ruststream::app]` writes: the command line (`run`, `asyncapi gen`) on a multi-threaded // Tokio runtime. fn main() -> ExitCode { run_main(app) }

The ruststream command runs a service and prints its AsyncAPI document through cargo run; cargo generate scaffolds a new one. ruststream run executes cargo run -- run against the crate's Cargo.toml, and ruststream asyncapi gen executes cargo run -- asyncapi gen. The service's own binary does the work: the main that #[ruststream::app] generates understands both commands. That main hands the commands to run_main, and the runtime::cli module documents them. cargo run -- run and cargo run -- asyncapi gen therefore give the same result without the command installed. The same run is one call from code. -p points at another crate or its Cargo.toml, and --release builds in release mode. asyncapi gen needs the service crate's asyncapi feature; the starter template enables it. The template's console logs come from its logging feature. cargo generate comes from the cargo-generate project; a broker crate ships templates of its own for its transport.

Install the command: cargo install ruststream --features cli Scaffold a service from the in-memory starter template: cargo generate --git https://github.com/powersemmi/ruststream templates/memory --name my-service cd my-service The template writes a crate whose main is generated by #[ruststream::app]: Cargo.toml src/main.rs src/orders.rs src/routes.rs Run it; Ctrl+C stops it gracefully: ruststream run Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 0.02s Running `target/debug/my-service run` 2026-10-16T07:49:57.254761Z INFO ruststream::lifecycle starting service service=my-service version=0.1.0 brokers=1 subscribers=2 2026-10-16T07:49:57.254790Z INFO ruststream::lifecycle broker connected broker="ruststream::memory::MemoryBroker" 2026-10-16T07:49:57.254844Z INFO ruststream::dispatch subscriber started subscriber=orders input="my_service::orders::Order" 2026-10-16T07:49:57.254854Z INFO ruststream::dispatch subscriber started subscriber=cancellations input="my_service::orders::Order" 2026-10-16T07:49:57.254859Z INFO ruststream::lifecycle service running subscribers=2 2026-10-16T07:50:00.281593Z INFO ruststream::lifecycle shutdown signal received 2026-10-16T07:50:00.281755Z INFO ruststream::lifecycle service stopped Print the AsyncAPI document: ruststream asyncapi gen Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 0.02s Running `target/debug/my-service asyncapi gen` { "asyncapi": "3.1.0", "info": { "title": "my-service", "version": "0.1.0" }, "defaultContentType": "application/json", "channels": { "cancellations": { "address": "cancellations", ... Write it as YAML, to a file, or for a crate in another directory: ruststream asyncapi gen --yaml ruststream asyncapi gen -o asyncapi.json ruststream asyncapi gen -p ../my-service

Four hooks run around the brokers' connection: on_startup, after_startup, on_shutdown and after_shutdown. on_startup runs before any broker connects. The value it returns becomes the application state, and its error aborts startup with no broker dialled. on_startup comes first in the builder: a hook registered before it makes the builder panic. after_startup runs once every subscription is open; its error aborts startup and shuts down the brokers that connected. on_shutdown runs when shutdown begins, while the brokers are still connected. after_shutdown runs after the brokers have shut down. The shutdown hooks' errors are logged and do not stop the shutdown. Every hook after on_startup receives the state as Arc<State>. shutdown_timeout bounds how long shutdown waits for handlers still running; past it, they are aborted. Without it, shutdown waits for them indefinitely. A broker scope's after_startup is a step of its mount chain, written before the includes, and receives a live publisher of that broker, paired from the policy it names. TestApp runs every hook in the service's order: the startup hooks on start, the shutdown hooks on shutdown.

A service runs until a signal, until a future of yours, or beside another server that owns the process.

health hands out a HealthProbe that reports whether a started service is running, stopping, stopped or failed, and how many of its subscriptions consume. The probe is a cheap clone, so each task that reports health holds its own. Its state is a HealthState: Running, ShuttingDown, Stopped or Failed with the fail-fast diagnostic. The probe outlives shutdown and keeps reporting the final state. stopping resolves when the service tears itself down after a fail-fast failure, so a server beside it can stop with it, as the HTTP page shows. subscriptions returns a SubscriptionCount: the subscriptions that consume and the subscriptions the service started. A subscription counts once, whatever its number of workers. The count changes only when a subscription starts or stops, so a delivery pays nothing for it.

examples/http_outbox.rs /// The liveness endpoint: the probe outlives `shutdown`, so this route reports the terminal /// state for as long as requests still reach it. Here that window is the graceful drain: a /// fail-fast also resolves the `stopping()` future below and stops the HTTP server. A host /// that should keep serving after the messaging side dies would omit that select arm. /// /// This service is unhealthy once a subscription stops consuming, even though the rest of it /// still runs: the orders it no longer reads would wait unanswered. async fn healthz(State(health): State<HealthProbe>) -> (StatusCode, String) { let count = health.subscriptions(); match health.state() { HealthState::Running if count.active == count.started => { (StatusCode::OK, "running".to_owned()) } HealthState::Running => ( StatusCode::SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE, format!( "{} of {} subscriptions consuming", count.active, count.started ), ), state => (StatusCode::SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE, format!("{state:?}")), } }

A subscription's stream can end while the service runs: the server cancels a consumer when its queue is deleted, or the broker gives up reconnecting. By default the subscription logs the end and stops, and the rest of the service runs on. The probe still reports Running and counts one subscription fewer, and the service decides whether that is healthy. on_subscription_end with SubscriptionEnd::FailFast makes the end a fail-fast failure instead. The service then shuts down gracefully, run returns an error that names the subscription, and the probe reports Failed. An end during shutdown is part of the shutdown and is never reported. examples/app_running.rs /// The service exists to answer orders, so a subscription whose stream ends while the /// service runs stops the service. fn app(broker: MemoryBroker) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .on_subscription_end(SubscriptionEnd::FailFast) .with_broker(broker, |b| b.include(issue_receipt).out_reply(Publish)) }

An HTTP server owns the process and the service runs beside it: started before the server, stopped after it. The service starts with start before the server accepts traffic, so a startup failure stops the process early. publisher pairs a bound token with its connected broker, for a task beside the service that publishes. The example's relay task publishes the orders an HTTP request stored in a transactional outbox. The server stops on Ctrl+C, or when stopping reports a fail-fast failure of the service. The service then drains with shutdown.

run starts the service and serves until SIGINT or SIGTERM, then shuts it down gracefully. run is the whole process: it connects the brokers, opens the subscriptions and runs the startup hooks, then waits for a signal. A startup failure is the error it returns. A signal starts the same shutdown a started service gets. A subscriber that fails fast tears the service down, and run returns that failure as its error. A subscription whose stream ends while the service runs does the same under SubscriptionEnd::FailFast. The main that #[ruststream::app] generates calls run.

examples/app_running.rs /// Runs the service until `SIGINT` or `SIGTERM`, then shuts it down gracefully. async fn serve_forever(broker: MemoryBroker) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { app(broker).run().await?; Ok(()) }

shutdown stops a started service gracefully: hooks, subscriptions, running handlers, then the brokers. shutdown runs on_shutdown, stops the subscriptions and waits for the handlers still running. It then shuts the brokers down in reverse order of registration and runs after_shutdown. The lifecycle page shows the hooks, and shutdown_timeout there bounds the wait for running handlers. A service that already tore itself down after a fail-fast failure returns that failure from shutdown. Dropping a RunningApp without shutdown detaches the service with no graceful shutdown.

examples/app_running.rs /// Stops a started service: the shutdown hooks run and the handlers in flight finish first. async fn stop(running: RunningApp) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let health = running.health(); running.shutdown().await?; tracing::info!(state = ?health.state(), "stopped"); Ok(()) }

start brings the service up and returns a RunningApp, so the caller owns the process and decides when it stops. start connects the brokers, opens the subscriptions and runs the startup hooks, then returns. A startup failure is the error start returns, before the caller accepts its own traffic. start installs no signal handlers: the caller stops the service with shutdown. The RunningApp also hands out the service's health and publishers for tasks beside it, as the HTTP page shows.

examples/app_running.rs /// Starts the service beside other work of the process, and stops it once that work is done. async fn serve( broker: MemoryBroker, work: impl Future<Output = ()> + Send, ) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { // `start` returns once every subscription is open. let running = app(broker).start().await?; work.await; running.shutdown().await?; Ok(()) }

run_until serves until a future of yours resolves, then shuts the service down gracefully. It starts the service the way run does, and installs no signal handlers. The future starts once the service has started, so it may publish to the service and wait for the answer. A subscriber that fails fast ends the run before the future resolves, and run_until returns that failure as its error.

examples/app_running.rs /// Runs the service until `work` resolves; `work` starts once the service has started. async fn serve_until( broker: MemoryBroker, work: impl Future<Output = ()> + Send, ) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { app(broker).run_until(work).await?; Ok(()) }
Shared state is one value built at startup that every handler reads, as a State<T> parameter or through a dependency-injection container.

on_startup builds one value of any type; a handler takes any of its fields as a State<T> parameter. on_startup runs once, before any broker connects, and its value becomes the application state. Its future can await: open a pool, connect a client, read a file. on_startup comes before with_broker, because it fixes the state type every handler is checked against. The lifecycle hooks after it receive the same state. #[derive(FromRef)] writes one FromRef impl per field, each cloning that field. A handler parameter State(prices): State<Prices> resolves through that impl before the body runs. A field that is expensive to clone goes behind an Arc, so a delivery pays one reference count. A handler can also borrow the whole state with ctx.state() from its &mut Context<'_, (), AppState> parameter, with no clone. A hand-written FromRef impl builds a value from several fields. A dependency-injection container fills the same role: froodi with RustStream support, or shaku wired by hand.

Macros Manual examples/app_state.rs /// A price list, loaded once at startup. #[derive(Clone)] struct Prices { per_item: u64, } /// The application state: each field is available to a handler as `State<FieldType>`. #[derive(FromRef)] struct AppState { prices: Prices, } #[subscriber("orders", reply)] async fn price(order: &Order, State(prices): State<Prices>) -> Receipt { Receipt { order_id: order.id, total: order.items * prices.per_item, } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .on_startup(async move |()| { Ok::<_, Infallible>(AppState { prices: Prices { per_item: 25 }, }) }) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| b.include(price).out_reply(Publish)) } examples/manual/app_state.rs /// A price list, loaded once at startup. #[derive(Clone)] struct Prices { per_item: u64, } /// The application state. struct AppState { prices: Prices, } // What `#[derive(FromRef)]` writes for each field: `State<Prices>` resolves through it. impl FromRef<AppState> for Prices { fn from_ref(state: &AppState) -> Self { state.prices.clone() } } struct Price; // The state type is the last parameter of `Handle`; the mount checks it against the app's. impl Handle<Order, Receipt, (), (), AppState> for Price { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), AppState>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Receipt, HandlerOutcome>> { let prices = Prices::from_ref(ctx.state()); ready(Ok(Receipt { order_id: order.id, total: order.items * prices.per_item, })) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .on_startup(async move |()| { Ok::<_, Infallible>(AppState { prices: Prices { per_item: 25 }, }) }) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Price).reply().build()) .out_reply(Publish) }) }

froodi (crates.io, docs.rs, GitHub) is a dependency-injection container whose ruststream feature builds a handler's dependencies per delivery, as Inject parameters. The registry declares each dependency with the scope it lives in. Config lives in the App scope, as long as the container. Pricing lives in the Request scope and is built from Config by its factory. ContainerLayer is a middleware, mounted with RustStream::layer: for every delivery it enters a child Request scope, runs the handler inside it and closes the scope once the handler has answered. Closing the scope runs the finalizers of what it built before the message is settled. Inject<Pricing> is a FromContext extractor that resolves from that child scope, so two parameters of one delivery share an instance. InjectTransient<T> builds a fresh instance for each parameter instead. A dependency the container cannot resolve drops the delivery and logs the channel and the type. A handler that takes Inject in a service with no ContainerLayer drops every delivery the same way. The layer builds a child container for every delivery, which allocates; dependencies in the App scope are built once. With froodi's async feature, AsyncContainerLayer holds a container whose factories and finalizers can await.

use froodi::{Container, DefaultScope, Inject, instance, registry}; use ruststream::memory::prelude::*; use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize}; #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] pub struct Order { pub id: u64, pub items: u64, } #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "receipts")] pub struct Receipt { pub order_id: u64, pub total: u64, } /// Lives as long as the application. #[derive(Clone)] pub struct Config { pub price_per_item: u64, } /// Built for every delivery from the configuration. pub struct Pricing { per_item: u64, } impl Pricing { fn total(&self, order: &Order) -> u64 { order.items * self.per_item } } fn container(config: Config) -> Container { Container::new(registry! { provide(DefaultScope::App, instance(config)), scope(DefaultScope::Request) [ provide(|Inject(config): Inject<Config>| Ok(Pricing { per_item: config.price_per_item, })), ], }) } #[subscriber("orders", reply)] async fn price(order: &Order, Inject(pricing): Inject<Pricing>) -> Receipt { Receipt { order_id: order.id, total: pricing.total(order), } } pub fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .layer(ContainerLayer::new(container(Config { price_per_item: 25, }))) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(price).out_reply(Publish) }) } Cargo.toml [dependencies] froodi = { version = "1.0.0-beta.19", features = ["ruststream"] } ruststream = { version = "0.8", default-features = false, features = ["memory", "json"] } schemars = "1" serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] } src/lib.rs use froodi::ruststream::ContainerLayer; shaku (crates.io, docs.rs, GitHub) is a dependency-injection container with no RustStream support; the service builds it in on_startup and a handler resolves from it. A shaku module is the container: module! lists its components, and each component implements an interface trait. on_startup builds the module with the components' parameters, and the module becomes the application state. A FromRef impl from the module to Arc<dyn Pricing> lets a handler take State<Arc<dyn Pricing>>, as for any struct as state. The module resolves a component as a clone of its Arc, so each delivery pays one reference count and the calls go through dyn Pricing. A handler that reads ctx.state().resolve_ref() borrows the component instead, with no reference count. Components are singletons of the module and are Send + Sync, so every handler on every worker shares them. An interface method that awaits needs a dyn-compatible form, such as one returning a boxed future.

TestApp runs a service's production app in process, drives its brokers and asserts on what its handlers received and published.
How a test publishes to a broker of the app and moves the app forward: settling deliveries and advancing time.

TestApp::advance lets a delay pass, fires the delayed redeliveries now due, and drives their reaction to a standstill. A handler that answers retry_after(delay) settles at once, and the publish returns with the delivery pending. advance(delay) then delivers the message again, by a broker's native delayed redelivery or by the runtime's deferred copy. In process it moves the paused clock, so the test starts paused with #[tokio::test(start_paused = true)]. On a running clock the in-process advance panics. In a start_live test it lets the time pass for real, because the delay is the broker's own timer. A copy the runtime publishes for a zero delay arrives in the same reaction, without advance. settle drives a reaction without moving the clock.

TestApp::broker addresses one broker of the app by its production type, for publishing to it and reading its records. B is the type the app registered, so MemoryBroker and MemoryBroker<Retaining> are two different brokers. The BrokerHandle it returns publishes onto that broker with message(&v) and opens its records: subscriber(name) and published::<T>(name). A subscription name is local to its broker: the "orders" of one broker is not the "orders" of the other. broker panics when the app has no broker of type B or more than one; two brokers of one type are addressed by label with broker_named. In live mode the test's input reaches the broker through its connected form's default publish policy.

TestApp::drain waits for the post-settle continuations of everything settled so far, for a test that asserts on their effects. A continuation is work a handler attaches to its outcome, ack().and_after(..), or to its context with after(..) or after_settle(..). It runs on its own task after the delivery settles, so a publish can return before it has finished. A settlement registers its continuations before it releases the delivery, so drain after a publish finds them all. An effect of the handler body itself needs no drain: the publish has already settled it. In the example the test builds the state with with_state to read the mail client's record afterwards. shutdown waits for continuations too.

message(&v) starts an input with the publish builder the service itself publishes through: destination, headers and codec. The value is an Outgoing type, and the type decides whether the builder still asks for a destination. A type that names its destination publishes there; a type that names none takes to(name). with_headers(&meta) adds a typed header contract, and with_codec(codec) encodes with another codec than the default one. publish() sends the input and drives the reaction, and with checks the value the handler received. TestApp::message publishes onto the app's only broker. With more than one broker it has no single target, so the publish fails with TestError::Ambiguous. tb.broker::<B>().message(..), the BrokerHandle::message of a broker chosen with broker::<B>() or broker_named, publishes onto that broker. A value whose type the test does not own goes through the shortcuts.

TestApp::settle drives a reaction the test started without the harness to a standstill, without publishing anything new. A publish through the harness settles for you; settle is for input that arrived some other way, such as a bare publisher of the broker. A batch handler needs it: each harness publish settles alone, so the batch it reaches holds one message. Two messages sent through a bare publisher wait together, and settle delivers them as one batch, which assert_batch_sizes reads back. In process settle waits until the transports report nothing in flight. In live mode it waits until every subscription has handled what the harness saw published to it, up to the deadline of start_live. advance settles after a delay has passed.

On the embassy runtime, TestApp runs a device service's EmbeddedApp on the host, with every broker connected in process and the clock the app reads in the test's hands. The test hands the app function its brokers, as the device's task does, and drives the app with the same calls a tokio test makes: broker, settle, advance and shutdown. The app runs inside the test's own future, so a test is a plain #[test] that blocks on one future, and one TestApp runs at a time in a process. The harness is the test build's embassy-time driver: the clock starts at zero and moves only when the test moves it. embassy-time's own mock-driver is a second driver of the same clock, and a build links only one of the two. TestApp::start returns once the app is running. A broker that waits on the clock to connect, or a subscription that waits to open, is waited for: the clock moves from one armed deadline to the next, and a startup nothing wakes returns TestError::Stalled. shutdown lets the work the app holds run to its end: the clock moves from one armed deadline to the next until the app has stopped. A handler or a hook that waits on a timer finishes, the shutdown hooks run and every broker shuts down. Work that waits on something nothing wakes makes shutdown return TestError::Stalled, and an app that stopped on its own error returns it as TestError::Failed.

tb.out::<M>() opens the record of the Out slot marked M: every message a handler sent through it, with its destination and headers. It reads the same way as on tokio, as the out page describes. A slot publish is also recorded on its destination, so published::<T>(name) on the broker it went to sees it.

on_call and on_publish take the same async closures as on tokio. A hook runs inside the test's own future: the dispatch that recorded the event waits for it, and the step that drives the app polls it beside the app. A hook runs on the test's own thread, and a hook that waits on the clock finishes once the test advances it or shuts the app down. A hook on a destination the test itself publishes to runs in that publish, up to where it waits on the clock. A panic inside a hook, a failed assertion included, fails the publish, settle, advance or shutdown that ran it.

TestApp::with_state(app, build) starts the app with the state build returns in place of the one the app was built with: a value read from the board's flash, a driver of its hardware. The app function names its state in its type, EmbeddedApp<impl Mounts<State = Limits>>, so the test can build one. The harness connects every broker first, then calls build with the brokers, so brokers.broker::<B>() returns the connected form of the app's broker of type B, as on tokio. Everything else of startup runs as in TestApp::start.

Hooks run a test's own code at the moment a subscription is called or a message is published.

on_call(hook) runs an async closure each time a subscription's handler is called, handing it the subscription's assertions as they stood at that call. The hook runs once per delivery, or once per batch, after the call settled. It gets the same SubscriberAssertions a test reads, with the new call already in the record, and without the calls recorded after it, so assert_called and settled work inside it. The publish that caused the call returns only after the hook finished. A hook that never finishes therefore hangs that publish; the test's timeout is the guard. A hook still running when the test shuts the harness down, or drops it, is stopped where it waits. A failed assertion inside the hook fails the publish, settle or advance that drove the call, and otherwise the test's shutdown or the end of the test. A hook applies from the moment it is registered, and several hooks on one subscription run in the order they were registered. It runs the same way under start_live.

on_publish(hook) runs an async closure each time a message is published to a destination, handing it that destination's assertions as they stood at that publish. It sees the test's own publishes and everything a publisher wired by the runtime sends: replies, Out slot publishes, retry copies and dead letters. On the record of a slot, out::<M>(), it runs for each publish through that slot. The hook gets PublishedAssertions with the new message already in the record and the later ones left out, so decoded and with work inside it. The record is the message as the framework handed it to the broker, in process and against a running stand alike. The publish the test made returns only after the hook finished, and a failed assertion inside the hook fails it, or else the test's shutdown or the end of the test. A hook applies from the moment it is registered, and several hooks on one destination run in the order they were registered.

Assertions on what was published to one destination: how many messages, their payloads, headers and per-message settings.

assert_called_once checks that exactly one message was published to the destination. The assertion counts the messages in the record, published::<T>(name), not the handler calls that produced them. It panics with the count it found when the record holds none or more than one. It returns the record, so with, with_raw and with_header chain after it. assert_called(n) checks any other count, and assert_not_called checks that nothing was published.

The records a test reads: what one subscriber received, what was published to a destination, and what went through an Out slot.

out::<M>() opens the record of one Out slot: every message the handler sent through it, on whichever broker it went. M is the slot's marker type, the one the handler names in Out<impl Publisher, M>, and it implements OutSlot. The record is attributed by slot, not by destination, so it shows which slot sent a message when two slots share a destination. published::<T>(name) is the record of one destination on one broker. Each entry keeps the destination name, the headers and the per-message settings of the publish, which with_options checks. The record is untyped: decoded_as::<U>() turns it into one that decodes to U. messages returns every entry for checks of your own. A publish made outside the handler task, such as a spawned task, is not attributed to the slot.

published::<T>(name) opens the record of one destination on a broker: every message published there, with its name and headers. T is the payload type that with and decoded decode to; the count and raw assertions ignore it. The assertions are those of PublishedAssertions, such as assert_called_once. In process the record is the broker's own publish log, so it holds replies, Out slot publishes, retry copies and the test's own publishes. out::<M>() shows what left through one slot, across brokers, and subscriber(name) is the record of a handler. Against a running stand it holds the test's publishes and everything a publisher wired by the runtime sent. The record is a snapshot taken when the method is called: call it after the publish that drives the reaction.

How a test starts the production app, gives it state, and shuts it down.

TestApp::shutdown tears the service down gracefully and returns what run would return, so a fail-fast failure fails the test. It is the service's own shutdown, step for step. It runs on_shutdown, stops the dispatch loops, and waits for in-flight handlers and post-settle continuations. It then shuts the brokers down in reverse order of registration and runs after_shutdown. The wait for handlers and continuations is bounded by the app's shutdown timeout. A failing shutdown hook is logged, and the shutdown goes on, as in the service. The result is Ok for a healthy run and RustStreamError::Dispatch after a fail-fast failure, such as a handler panic under the default policy. A broker that fails to shut down returns the service's error for it too. run_result gives the same result while the harness is still running, and assert_shut_down asserts the failure. shutdown takes the harness by value, so nothing can be published after it.

start_live connects the brokers of the same app to a running stand, so one test body checks the service against the real broker. It is for a stand of a networked broker: a Kafka or NATS server the test suite starts beside the tests. Each broker connects through its ordinary connect, and the rest of startup is the production one. The test body is the one an in-process test runs; only the start call differs from TestApp::start. MemoryBroker connects without a server, so the example runs in process in every mode. A publish, settle and advance wait on the real clock until every subscription has handled what was published to it. The wait lasts ten seconds at most; start_live_within sets another bound, and past it the call fails with TestError::NotSettled naming the subscription. A live test runs on the real clock: start_live on a paused clock fails with TestError::PausedClock. The test's input reaches the broker through its connected form's default publish policy.

TestApp::start runs the app main builds, unchanged, with every broker connected in process and no server. The harness starts the app in the service's own order: on_startup, then each broker's connect, then the subscriptions, then after_startup. Each broker connects through its in-process transition, which performs no I/O and yields the broker's production connected form. MemoryBroker has no server, so its in-process mode is its ordinary connect. A networked broker provides the in-process mode under its crate's testing feature, which a service enables in [dev-dependencies]. A broker without it makes start fail with TestError::NoTransport naming the broker. A failing on_startup fails start with TestError::Startup before any broker connects. start_live runs the same app against a running stand, and with_state starts it with a state the test builds. A test ends with shutdown.

TestBrokers::broker::<B>() returns the connected form of the app's broker of type B. A publisher built from it publishes onto the bus the assertions read, such as published::<T>(name) and its with. The app's on_startup does not run; after_startup and everything else of startup do, as in TestApp::start. TestBrokers::broker panics when the app has no broker of type B or more than one.

Assertions on one subscriber: how often it ran, what it received and how each delivery was settled.

assert_batch_sizes(&[..]) checks how a subscriber's deliveries were cut into handler calls. Each number is the size of one call, in call order. The mount names the largest size, batch(nonzero!(2)); the broker builds the batches, and this reads back what it built. One batch is one call, so five orders in batches of two make assert_called(3). A single-message handler is called per delivery, so three deliveries read [1, 1, 1]. The batches come from a replayed log, as on the batches page. A batch built from a bare publisher is driven with settle.

assert_called_once checks that a subscriber's handler ran exactly once: one delivery, or one batch. It counts handler calls in the record, subscriber(name), not messages: a batch handler called with five orders counts once. A delivery that did not decode counts too: the record holds it although the body never ran. It returns the assertions, so with, with_raw and settled chain after it and read that one call. On failure it panics with the number of calls it found. assert_called(n) checks any other number, and assert_not_called checks that there was no call.

assert_called(n) checks that a subscriber's handler ran exactly n times, counting a batch as one call. n is the number of handler calls. A single-message handler is called once per delivery, and once more for each redelivery. A batch handler is called once per batch, so here n counts batches; assert_batch_sizes shows how big each one was. A publish through the harness runs to completion before it returns, so three publishes make three calls. On failure it panics with the number of calls it found. assert_called_once is the same check for one call, and outcomes shows how each call settled. A destination's assert_called(n) counts publishes instead.

assert_last_failed_to_decode() checks that the latest delivery did not decode into the handler's input type. The verdict comes from the codec, or from the broker when its client reports a decode error itself. The record holds the delivery as a call although the body never ran, so assert_called_once counts it. The decode policy settles it: the default drops the message and keeps the service running, which assert_running states. The test injects the bad bytes through a #[derive(Outgoing, Serialized)] newtype, which publishes them as they are. It returns nothing, so it ends a chain. assert_outcome gives the same verdict as Outcome::DecodeFailed, and panicked checks the other failure a call can end in.

assert_not_called checks that a subscriber's handler never ran. It passes when the record of that subscription, subscriber(name), is empty. A name no handler subscribes to has an empty record as well, so a misspelled name passes. A positive check on a neighbour guards against that: here assert_called_once on "orders" shows the order did arrive. The handler sends only an order without an id on to "rejected", so a valid order leaves the review subscription untouched. It returns nothing, so it ends a chain. assert_called(n) expects any number of calls.

assert_outcome(..) checks the latest handler call by its classified Outcome, failures included. Outcome folds a call into five cases: Ack, Nack, Drop, DecodeFailed and Panicked. Nack covers both retry() and retry_after(..), so the delay plays no part. A panic or a decode failure wins over the settlement: such a call reads as Panicked or DecodeFailed, which panicked and assert_last_failed_to_decode check on their own. Here the delayed copy waits for tb.advance(..) on the paused clock, so the record holds one call. settled checks by HandlerOutcome instead, and outcomes returns the outcome of every call.

batches_raw() returns the bytes a batch handler received, one list per call. It is received_raw with the batch boundaries kept. A single-message handler yields lists of one. Here the handler takes raw frames, &[Frame<'_>], so no codec runs on the way in or in the check. The batches come from a replayed log, as on the batches page. A batch built from a bare publisher is driven with settle.

batches::<T>() returns what a batch handler received, one decoded list per call. Each inner list is one handler call, in call order, so the batch boundaries that received drops stay. It decodes with DefaultCodec; batches_with(&codec) decodes with another codec. A publish through the harness runs each message to completion on its own, so it reaches a batch handler as a batch of one. Fuller batches come from a log that already holds the messages: the test fills a retaining broker, the subscription opens at the start of its log, and tb.settle() drives the replay. The settle page shows a batch built from a bare publisher. The mount names the size, batch(nonzero!(2)), so three orders arrive as two and one. batches_raw returns the same batches as bytes, and assert_batch_sizes checks only the sizes.

outcomes() returns how every handler call settled, in call order. Each entry is an Outcome: Ack, Nack, Drop, DecodeFailed or Panicked. settled and assert_outcome read the latest call only; outcomes pins a sequence, such as a nack followed by the ack of its redelivery. A batch call has one entry, classified by its first delivery. Outcome is #[non_exhaustive], so a match on it needs a wildcard arm.

panicked() checks that the handler panicked on its latest call. The harness runs dispatch under the app's real failure policy. Under the default policy, fail_fast, a panic shuts the service down, which tb.assert_shut_down() states. The delivery stays unsettled, so no settled(..) matches it; assert_outcome(Outcome::Panicked) is the same check by outcome. The test output carries the handler's panic message, and the test itself passes. assert_last_failed_to_decode checks the other failure a call can end in. The assert_shut_down and run_result pages show what the panic did to the service.

received::<T>() returns every payload a subscriber received, decoded with the default codec, for a check of your own. The list is flat and in delivery order: a batch contributes each of its elements. batches keeps the same payloads grouped by call. It decodes with DefaultCodec; received_with(&codec) decodes with another codec. Every recorded payload must decode as T, so a delivery that failed to decode makes it panic. It fits a check that a chain of assertions cannot say: an order, a subset, a property of every element. with checks the latest payload only, and received_raw returns the same list as bytes.

settled(outcome) checks how the latest handler call settled, against the HandlerOutcome a handler returns. It takes the value a handler answers with: ack(), retry(), drop(), retry_after(..). It compares the settlement alone, so a hook attached with and_after plays no part. For a batch it checks every element of the latest call, which is what one answer for the whole slice produces. The record holds what the handler answered: on a transport that cannot requeue, a retry still reads as a retry, and the missing redelivery shows in assert_called. A fail-fast panic leaves the delivery unsettled, which matches no outcome. assert_outcome is the same check by Outcome, failures included, and outcomes returns every settlement in order.

with_value(&value) checks the value the latest delivery lent its handler, on a broker whose deliveries already hold one. Some brokers decode a delivery in their client and lend the handler that value, such as a database row; the delivery implements Carries<T>. That value never was bytes, so with has nothing to decode; the harness keeps a clone of the lent value instead. The value type needs Clone, PartialEq and Debug. It panics when the latest delivery lent no T: the handler takes another type, or the delivery carried nothing. The row subscription here stands in for such a broker crate: it reads id:name payloads of the in-memory broker as rows (examples/support/carried_rows.rs). received_values returns every lent value, not only the latest.

with(&value) checks that the latest handler call received this value, decoded with the default codec. It reads the most recent call only; the earlier ones are in received. It decodes the recorded payload with DefaultCodec, the codec the enabled features select (json first). A handler mounted with another codec is checked with with_codec(&codec, &value), which decodes with that codec. The value type needs Deserialize, PartialEq and Debug. The latest call must hold one delivery: on a batch of several it panics, and the batch is read with batches. with_raw checks the same call as bytes, and with_value the value a carrying delivery lent the handler. A destination's with checks the value a publish carried.

The asyncapi feature generates the AsyncAPI 3.1 document of a service from its app value, with build_spec. The document is read from what the app registers, so it describes the handlers the service mounts and nothing else. It lists the channels and operations, the message schemas, the servers and who owns the service. It is built on demand, from a test, a command or an HTTP route, and costs the running service nothing.

How the document is produced, serialized and served, and where its payload schemas come from. build_spec reads the document from the app value, and the document serializes to JSON or YAML.
