The main that the app attribute generates prints it, and a self-contained page renders it. Payload schemas come from a JsonSchema derive on each message type.

build_spec reads the AsyncAPI document of a service from its app value, the same value main runs. The document follows AsyncAPI 3.1. It is read from what the app registers, so it describes the handlers the service mounts and nothing else. Each subscriber becomes a channel named after its subscription, a receive operation, and a message component for its input type. The handler's doc comment is the operation's description, and the input type's doc comment is the message's. A reply rides the receive operation, and each message an Out slot declares gets a send operation. The result is a Spec: plain data with public fields, which a test reads and a tool may complete before it is serialized. The document is built when the function is called, so it costs the running service nothing. The asyncapi feature turns it on. The example runs with cargo test --example asyncapi_generation --features macros,memory,asyncapi.

Macros Manual examples/asyncapi_generation.rs /// Accepts every order placed in the shop. #[subscriber("orders")] async fn accept(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, item = %order.item, "accepted"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| b.include(accept)) } /// The document of the service, read from the same app value `main` runs. fn document() -> Spec { build_spec(&app()) } examples/manual/asyncapi_generation.rs /// The handler `#[subscriber("orders")]` writes for the body. struct Accept; impl Handle<Order> for Accept { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, item = %order.item, "accepted"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include( subscriber("orders", Accept) .describe("Accepts every order placed in the shop.") .build(), ) }) } /// The document of the service, read from the same app value `main` runs. fn document() -> Spec { build_spec(&app()) }

asyncapi gen prints the document of a service from the main that #[ruststream::app] generates. The command builds the app with the builder the attribute names and prints what build_spec returns. It prints JSON by default; --yaml prints YAML, and -o <file> writes to a file instead of standard output. The service crate enables the asyncapi feature; without it the command fails with an error that names the feature. The ruststream command runs it through cargo run against a crate, and cargo run -- asyncapi gen does the same without it. A main written by hand gets the same commands from run_main.
In the service crate: cargo run -- asyncapi gen cargo run -- asyncapi gen --yaml -o asyncapi.yaml With the ruststream command installed: ruststream asyncapi gen -o asyncapi.json

.describe(text) gives a manual registration the operation description the attribute takes from the handler's doc comment. describe is a step of the subscriber(..) chain, before .build(); after .reply() it is still available. The text becomes the description of the registration's receive operation. A message's description comes from its own type. A message whose type has no description takes the handler's. On the attribute path the doc comment of the handler function is the description, and the step has no use. The example runs with cargo test --example asyncapi_generation --features macros,memory,asyncapi.

Macros Manual examples/asyncapi_generation.rs /// Accepts every order placed in the shop. #[subscriber("orders")] async fn accept(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, item = %order.item, "accepted"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/asyncapi_generation.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include( subscriber("orders", Accept) .describe("Accepts every order placed in the shop.") .build(), ) }) }

MessageInfo names the component of a message in the document and describes it, whatever the Rust type is called. Channels and operations refer to a message by its component name. Without MessageInfo that name is the schema's title, which schemars takes from the type's name, so renaming the type renames the published message. An impl of MessageInfo keeps the name: NAME is the component's name and DESCRIPTION its description. #[derive(MessageInfo)] writes the impl from the type's name and doc comment. With #[message(headers(Meta))] the derive also declares the type's header contract. #[derive(Outgoing)] implements MessageInfo for the types it derives. Without the macros a registration names the component by the schema's title, so #[schemars(rename = "..")] keeps the published name there. The example runs with cargo test --example asyncapi_schemas --features macros,memory,asyncapi.

Macros Manual examples/asyncapi_schemas.rs /// A refund a customer asked for. #[derive(Debug, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] struct RefundRequestV2 { order_id: u64, } /// The component keeps the name the contract was published under, whatever the type is called. impl MessageInfo for RefundRequestV2 { const NAME: &'static str = "RefundRequest"; const DESCRIPTION: Option<&'static str> = Some("A refund a customer asked for."); } #[subscriber("refunds")] async fn refund(request: &RefundRequestV2) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(request.order_id, "refund requested"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/asyncapi_schemas.rs /// A refund a customer asked for. // The schema's title names the component: the rename keeps the name the contract was published // under, whatever the type is called. #[derive(Debug, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(rename = "RefundRequest")] struct RefundRequestV2 { order_id: u64, } struct Refund; impl Handle<RefundRequestV2> for Refund { fn handle( &self, request: &RefundRequestV2, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(request.order_id, "refund requested"); ready(Ok(())) } }

messages_without_schema lists the messages the document describes with no payload schema, for a check to fail on. A message without a schema documents its channel but not its shape, and a client generator has no type to produce from it. build_spec logs one warning per gap when it builds the document; this method returns the same list as component names. A test or a release check asserts on it. Messages whose bytes are their own format, on a byte lane, are left out: they have no schema by design. On the attribute path a gap is a message type without a JsonSchema derive. A subscriber(..) registration has one only after undocumented. The example runs with cargo test --example asyncapi_schemas --features macros,memory,asyncapi.

Macros Manual examples/asyncapi_schemas.rs /// An audit record another team publishes, with no schema shipped for it. #[derive(Debug, Deserialize)] struct AuditRecord { action: String, } #[subscriber("audit")] async fn record(entry: &AuditRecord) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(action = %entry.action, "audited"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// The release check: every message in the document has a schema, or the check names the ones /// that do not. fn check_schemas(spec: &Spec) -> Result<(), String> { match spec.messages_without_schema().as_slice() { [] => Ok(()), gaps => Err(format!("no payload schema for {}", gaps.join(", "))), } } examples/manual/asyncapi_schemas.rs /// An audit record another team publishes, with no schema shipped for it. #[derive(Debug, Deserialize)] struct AuditRecord { action: String, } struct Record; impl Handle<AuditRecord> for Record { fn handle( &self, entry: &AuditRecord, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(action = %entry.action, "audited"); ready(Ok(())) } } /// The release check: every message in the document has a schema, or the check names the ones /// that do not. fn check_schemas(spec: &Spec) -> Result<(), String> { match spec.messages_without_schema().as_slice() { [] => Ok(()), gaps => Err(format!("no payload schema for {}", gaps.join(", "))), } }

A message type that derives JsonSchema gives its message a payload schema in the document. The crate re-exports schemars as ruststream::schemars, so a service needs no dependency of its own for the derive. The schema is JSON Schema draft 07, the draft the AsyncAPI Schema Object extends. Doc comments on the type and its fields become descriptions in the schema, and the type's doc comment is the message's description. serde attributes shape the schema as they shape the wire: a renamed field or an Option reads the same in both. On the attribute path the derive is optional. A type without it still mounts, and its message carries no payload schema. build_spec then logs a warning naming the subscription and the type, and messages_without_schema lists the message. A subscriber(..) registration demands the derive at compile time; undocumented lifts the demand from one registration. A type that carries its own bytes, on a byte lane, has no schema by design and is not listed as missing one. The example runs with cargo test --example asyncapi_schemas --features macros,memory,asyncapi.

Macros Manual examples/asyncapi_schemas.rs /// An order placed by a customer. #[derive(Debug, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] struct Order { /// The order number, unique per shop. id: u64, /// What was ordered. item: String, /// How many items; one when absent. quantity: Option<u32>, } #[subscriber("orders")] async fn accept(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, item = %order.item, quantity = ?order.quantity, "accepted"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/asyncapi_schemas.rs /// An order placed by a customer. #[derive(Debug, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] struct Order { /// The order number, unique per shop. id: u64, /// What was ordered. item: String, /// How many items; one when absent. quantity: Option<u32>, } /// The handler `#[subscriber("orders")]` writes for the body. struct Accept; impl Handle<Order> for Accept { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, item = %order.item, quantity = ?order.quantity, "accepted"); ready(Ok(())) } }

to_json and to_yaml serialize the document in the two formats AsyncAPI tools read. to_json writes pretty-printed JSON, and to_yaml writes YAML. Each returns its serializer's error; a document build_spec built serializes without one. Servers, channels, operations and components are maps sorted by name, so the output is the same on every run and a change reads as a plain diff in review. The command the generated main understands prints the same text. The example runs with cargo test --example asyncapi_generation --features macros,memory,asyncapi.

examples/asyncapi_generation.rs /// Writes the document next to the service's code, in both formats AsyncAPI tools read. fn write_document(dir: &Path) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let spec = build_spec(&app()); fs::write(dir.join("asyncapi.json"), spec.to_json()?)?; fs::write(dir.join("asyncapi.yaml"), spec.to_yaml()?)?; Ok(()) }

.undocumented() takes the schemas of one manual registration out of the document and lifts its JsonSchema demand. Under the asyncapi feature a subscriber(..) registration is documented by default. Mounting it demands JsonSchema of its message types, and a type without the derive is a compile error at the mount. undocumented is the exit for one registration, such as one whose message type comes from a crate that ships no schema. The registration stays in the document: its channel and its operation remain, and its messages carry no payload schema. messages_without_schema lists those messages. The step is written once; a second one does not compile. On the attribute path a type without the derive already mounts and contributes no schema, so the attribute has no such step. Without the asyncapi feature a registration demands nothing. The example runs with cargo test --example asyncapi_schemas --features macros,memory,asyncapi.

Macros Manual examples/asyncapi_schemas.rs /// An audit record another team publishes, with no schema shipped for it. #[derive(Debug, Deserialize)] struct AuditRecord { action: String, } #[subscriber("audit")] async fn record(entry: &AuditRecord) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(action = %entry.action, "audited"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/asyncapi_schemas.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Accept).build()) .include(subscriber("refunds", Refund).build()) // `AuditRecord` has no `JsonSchema`: without this step the mount does not compile. .include(subscriber("audit", Record).undocumented().build()) }) }

render_viewer_html returns a self-contained HTML page that renders the document with the AsyncAPI React component. The page loads the document from the URL it is given, so the service serves two routes: the document and the page. The function renders a string; serving it is the job of the HTTP stack the service already runs. examples/asyncapi_http.rs in the repository serves both routes with axum. The component and its stylesheet load from jsDelivr, at a pinned version. ViewerOptions sets the page title and another asset base with cdn_base: a mirror, or the service's own assets where the network has no way out. The example runs with cargo test --example asyncapi_generation --features macros,memory,asyncapi.

examples/asyncapi_generation.rs /// The page the service serves at `/docs`: it renders the document served at `/asyncapi.json`. fn docs_page() -> String { let options = ViewerOptions::default().title("Orders events"); render_viewer_html("/asyncapi.json", &options) }

What the document says about a service beyond its channels: replies, channel parameters, headers, content types and retries. Each of them comes from a declaration the runtime already acts on, so the document and the service's behaviour do not drift apart.

A destination declared as a name template becomes a channel whose address keeps its placeholders, each one declared as a parameter. #[outgoing(name = "orders.{tenant}.accepted")] declares a name template. The template is the channel's id and its address. Each {placeholder} is an entry of the channel's parameters. The document names the segments; what a service puts in them is run-time data and is not listed. A type reaches the document where it is published: each type of an Out slot's #[publishes(..)] list gets a send operation on its channel. A type with no declared destination contributes no channel, since each call site names its own. Without the macros the slot's OutSlot::outgoing returns the list, and OutgoingMessageMetadata::with_parameters names the placeholders. The example runs with cargo test --example asyncapi_reports --features macros,memory,asyncapi.

Macros Manual examples/asyncapi_reports.rs /// An order accepted for one tenant: the tenant is a segment of the channel's name. #[derive(Debug, Serialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] #[outgoing(name = "orders.{tenant}.accepted")] struct Accepted { id: u64, } #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Accepted)] struct Tenants; #[subscriber("orders")] async fn accept(order: &Order, Out(tenants): Out<impl Publisher, Tenants>) -> HandlerOutcome { let accepted = Accepted { id: order.id }; match tenants .message(&accepted) .to() .tenant(&order.tenant) .publish() .await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(_) => HandlerOutcome::retry(), } } examples/manual/asyncapi_reports.rs /// An order accepted for one tenant: the tenant is a segment of the channel's name. #[derive(Debug, Serialize, JsonSchema)] struct Accepted { id: u64, } impl OutgoingDestination for Accepted { type Form = NameTemplate; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "orders.{tenant}.accepted"; const PARAMETERS: &'static [&'static str] = &["tenant"]; } impl MessageHeaders for Accepted { type Contract = NoHeaders; } impl<Cont> TemplateAddress<Cont> for Accepted { type Builder = AcceptedAt<Cont, MissingSegment<Tenant>>; fn begin(cont: Cont) -> Self::Builder { AcceptedAt { cont, tenant: MissingSegment::new(), } } } /// The slot the handler publishes through, and the dictionary the document reports for it. struct Tenants; impl OutSlot for Tenants { const NAME: &'static str = "Tenants"; type Destination = Reads; fn outgoing() -> Vec<OutgoingMessageMetadata> { <Accepted as OutMessages<Self>>::outgoing() } } impl PublishedThrough<Tenants> for Accepted {} impl<M: OutSlot> OutMessages<M> for Accepted { fn outgoing() -> Vec<OutgoingMessageMetadata> { vec![ OutgoingMessageMetadata::new(Self::DESTINATION, type_name::<Self>()) .with_parameters(Self::PARAMETERS) .with_payload_schema(<Self as Documentable>::schema_json()), ] } } struct Accept; impl<O> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(O,)>> for Accept where O: OutEntry<Tenants, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(O,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let accepted = Accepted { id: order.id }; let tenants = outs.get(Tenants); match tenants .message(&accepted) .to() .tenant(&order.tenant) .publish() .await { Ok(()) => Ok(()), Err(_) => Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()), } } }

Each message names the media type of the codec that reads or writes it; the root defaultContentType appears only when all of them agree. The media type is the codec's CONTENT_TYPE: application/json, application/cbor or application/msgpack. It follows the codec chosen for the mounting, at whichever level chose it. A message that no codec reads or writes names none: a type that carries its own bytes, on a byte lane. A reader applies the root defaultContentType to each message that names no media type. So it stands only while every message names the same one; a second format, or a message without one, leaves it out. A message shared by several registrations takes the media type of the first.

The example needs the cbor feature: cargo test --example asyncapi_content_type --features macros,memory,asyncapi,cbor Macros Manual examples/asyncapi_content_type.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("plant", "0.1.0")) // The default codec: `Order` is `application/json`. .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| b.include(accept)) // The scope's codec: `Reading` is `application/cbor`. .with_broker_codec(MemoryBroker::new(), CborCodec, |b| b.include(record)) } examples/manual/asyncapi_content_type.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("plant", "0.1.0")) // The default codec: `Order` is `application/json`. .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Accept).build()) }) // The scope's codec: `Reading` is `application/cbor`. .with_broker_codec(MemoryBroker::new(), CborCodec, |b| { b.include(subscriber("readings", Record).build()) }) }

A header contract becomes the headers schema of its message, from a Headers<T> parameter or from #[outgoing(headers = ..)]. The contract struct derives JsonSchema, as a payload does. The schema describes the logical contract; on the wire each header value is a string (see Headers). On the receive side the contract is a Headers<T> parameter, or the header half of a Message<H, P> input. On the publish side it is the type's #[outgoing(headers = Meta)] declaration. A message component carries one contract. Two handlers that read one type with different contracts keep the first, and generation logs a warning. Without the macros a Message<H, P> input reports its contract. The example runs with cargo test --example asyncapi_reports --features macros,memory,asyncapi.

Macros Manual examples/asyncapi_reports.rs /// What travels in the headers of a shipment. #[derive(Debug, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] struct ShipmentMeta { /// The trace the shipment belongs to. trace_id: String, /// The carrier's attempt number. attempt: u32, } /// A parcel handed to the carrier. #[derive(Debug, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] struct Shipment { id: u64, } #[subscriber("shipments")] async fn ship(shipment: &Shipment, Headers(meta): Headers<ShipmentMeta>) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(shipment.id, trace_id = %meta.trace_id, meta.attempt, "shipped"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/asyncapi_reports.rs /// What travels in the headers of a shipment. #[derive(Debug, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] struct ShipmentMeta { /// The trace the shipment belongs to. trace_id: String, /// The carrier's attempt number. attempt: u32, } /// A parcel handed to the carrier. #[derive(Debug, Deserialize, JsonSchema)] struct Shipment { id: u64, } /// The pair input carries the header contract, so the registration reports its schema. struct Ship; impl Handle<Message<ShipmentMeta, Shipment>> for Ship { fn handle( &self, shipment: &Message<ShipmentMeta, Shipment>, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { let meta = &shipment.headers; tracing::info!(shipment.body.id, trace_id = %meta.trace_id, meta.attempt, "shipped"); ready(Ok(())) } }

A subscription over an InMessages set lists one message per variant, each with its own name, description, headers and content type. The receive operation names every model of the set, and the channel carries one message component per model. A serde model reports the content type of the codec of the mount and its payload schema; a model that reads its own bytes reports neither, by design, and is not counted by messages_without_schema. Under the header rule each message's headers schema carries the header with its const value, the counterpart of an OpenAPI discriminator mapping, so a reader of the document knows which header picks which message. A model with a header contract of its own keeps it, and the rule's header joins its properties; a Headers<T> parameter of the handler joins every model's schema the same way. A model that two sets name with different header values keeps the first value in the document, and generation logs a warning, as for two header contracts on one type. A dead-letter or retry destination of such a subscription lists the same models. The example runs with cargo test --example in_messages --features testing,macros,memory,asyncapi.

Macros Manual examples/in_messages.rs /// Every event of an order on the `orders` subscription: the `event` header names the model. #[derive(InMessages)] #[in_messages(header = "event")] enum OrderEvent { #[in_messages(value = "created")] Created(OrderCreated), #[in_messages(value = "cancelled")] Cancelled(OrderCancelled), } examples/manual/in_messages.rs /// Every event of an order on the `orders` subscription: the `event` header names the model. enum OrderEvent { Created(OrderCreated), Cancelled(OrderCancelled), } /// The kinds of the set, what a discriminator names; the derive generates this enum. #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)] enum OrderEventKind { Created, Cancelled, } impl InMessages for OrderEvent { type Kind = OrderEventKind; fn decode<DecodeCodec, M>(codec: &DecodeCodec, msg: &M) -> Result<Self, CodecError> where DecodeCodec: Codec, M: IncomingMessage, { let kind = match msg.headers().get("event") { Some(b"created") => OrderEventKind::Created, Some(b"cancelled") => OrderEventKind::Cancelled, Some(other) => { return Err(CodecError::Decode( format!( "the `event` header is `{}`, which names no variant of `OrderEvent`", String::from_utf8_lossy(other) ) .into(), )); } None => { return Err(CodecError::Decode( "the delivery carries no `event` header".into(), )); } }; // The chosen variant decodes once, through its model's own path. let payload = msg.payload(); match kind { OrderEventKind::Created => { <OrderCreated as InVariant<Self>>::decode_variant(codec, payload) .map(OrderEvent::Created) } OrderEventKind::Cancelled => { <OrderCancelled as InVariant<Self>>::decode_variant(codec, payload) .map(OrderEvent::Cancelled) } } } // One entry per model, in the order of the variants, each with the header value that names // it; the document lists them as the messages of the subscription. fn incoming() -> Vec<IncomingMessageMetadata> { vec![ <OrderCreated as InVariant<Self>>::describe() .with_discriminator(HeaderDiscriminator::new("event", "created")), <OrderCancelled as InVariant<Self>>::describe() .with_discriminator(HeaderDiscriminator::new("event", "cancelled")), ] } } impl Input for OrderEvent { type Axis = SoloSet<Self>; }

A reply is the reply of the receive operation it answers: the document names its channel and its message. A request-reply registration's receive operation carries a reply object. It points at the reply's channel and at the reply type's message component. The reply gets no send operation of its own. Its channel is the destination the reply resolves to: the reply type's #[outgoing(name = "..")], or the name the mount site gives (see Replies). A reply that a naming transform addresses per delivery has no fixed address, and its channel's address is null. The reply's address then says where a client reads it, as a runtime expression such as $message.header#/reply-to. The broker states that expression through PublishPolicy::reply_address_location, and a broker that cannot state it leaves the address out. The example runs with cargo test --example asyncapi_reports --features macros,memory,asyncapi.

Macros Manual examples/asyncapi_reports.rs /// The confirmation an order request gets back. #[derive(Debug, Serialize, Outgoing, JsonSchema)] struct Confirmed { id: u64, } /// Confirms every order request. #[subscriber("order-requests", reply("confirmations"))] async fn confirm(order: &Order) -> Confirmed { Confirmed { id: order.id } } examples/manual/asyncapi_reports.rs /// The confirmation an order request gets back. #[derive(Debug, Serialize, JsonSchema)] struct Confirmed { id: u64, } // `#[derive(Outgoing)]` with no `name`, by hand: the chain names the destination. impl OutgoingDestination for Confirmed { type Form = CallerName; } impl MessageHeaders for Confirmed { type Contract = NoHeaders; } struct Confirm; impl Handle<Order, Confirmed> for Confirm { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Confirmed, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(Confirmed { id: order.id })) } }

The attempt cap and the dead-letter destination of a registration appear on its receive operation as the x-ruststream-retry extension. max_attempts(n) is maxAttempts, and dead_letter(name) is deadLetter. AsyncAPI has a field for neither: a binding models a dead-letter queue only for SQS and SNS, and nothing models an attempt cap. So the document carries them as an extension of the operation. The dead-letter destination is a channel of its own, with a send operation, since the registration publishes there. Retry copies sent to a named destination add retryDestination, with its channel (see Retry slot). Copies that return to the subscription's own address add nothing: that channel is already in the document. A registration that declares none of this has no extension. The example runs with cargo test --example asyncapi_reports --features macros,memory,asyncapi.

Macros Manual examples/asyncapi_reports.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(confirm) .include(accept) .out(Tenants, Publish) .include(ship) // The cap and the dead-letter destination reach the document with the registration. .include(charge) .max_attempts(nonzero!(3u32)) .dead_letter("payments.dead") }) } examples/manual/asyncapi_reports.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include( subscriber("order-requests", Confirm) .describe("Confirms every order request.") .reply() .to("confirmations") .build(), ) .include(subscriber("orders", Accept).build()) .out(Tenants, Publish) .include(subscriber("shipments", Ship).build()) // The cap and the dead-letter destination reach the document with the registration. .include(subscriber("payments", Charge).build()) .max_attempts(nonzero!(3u32)) .dead_letter("payments.dead") }) }

The servers section: the brokers a service connects to, how clients authenticate, and the protocol bindings. A broker registered under a label describes its own server. The service declares the others, and states how clients authenticate to each.

Bindings carry what one protocol says about a server, a channel, an operation or a message, in that protocol's AsyncAPI vocabulary. A Binding is one protocol's object. Binding::new takes the protocol key, the binding's version and a serde body, and writes bindingVersion into the body itself. A key outside the specification's list fails construction with a BindingError, at startup rather than in a published file. Binding::extension carries an x- object for a transport the specification has no binding for. Bindings holds one body per protocol, and an empty set leaves the object out of the document. Broker crates fill most bindings: a server through DescribeServer, a subscription through its descriptor's channel_bindings and its siblings, a publish position through its PublishPolicy. A service attaches a server binding itself with ServerSpec::bindings. The example runs with cargo test --example asyncapi_servers --features macros,memory,asyncapi.

examples/asyncapi_servers.rs /// The Kafka server binding: where the cluster's schema registry is. #[derive(Serialize)] struct KafkaServer { #[serde(rename = "schemaRegistryUrl")] schema_registry_url: &'static str, } /// Adds the binding; a protocol the specification does not list fails here, at startup. fn with_registry(server: ServerSpec) -> Result<ServerSpec, BindingError> { let registry = KafkaServer { schema_registry_url: "https://registry.example.com", }; let binding = Binding::new("kafka", "0.5.0", &registry)?; Ok(server.bindings(Bindings::new().with(binding))) }

ServerSpec::security attaches a SecurityScheme that says how clients authenticate; each scheme becomes a component the server references. Security is the service author's statement, never the broker's: one broker runs with different authentication in different deployments. To secure a server a labeled broker describes, the service declares it again under the same label with the scheme attached. Each call of security adds an alternative, in order. The first scheme's component takes the server's name as its key, the next ones -1, -2 and on. SecurityScheme has a constructor per scheme the specification lists: user_password, api_key with an ApiKeyLocation, x509, plain, scram_sha256, scram_sha512, gssapi, http, http_api_key with an HttpApiKeyLocation, open_id_connect and oauth2. custom takes a scheme object as JSON, and description adds a note. The example runs with cargo test --example asyncapi_servers --features macros,memory,asyncapi.

examples/asyncapi_servers.rs /// How clients authenticate: SCRAM over TLS, or a client certificate. fn secured(server: ServerSpec) -> ServerSpec { server .security(SecurityScheme::scram_sha512().description("SASL over TLS")) .security(SecurityScheme::x509()) }

RustStream::server declares a server the document lists, from a ServerSpec that says how clients reach the broker. server is for a broker no registration of the process describes, or to replace what a labeled broker says. The name is the server's key in the document. ServerSpec::new takes the host and the protocol. ServerSpec::from_url takes a broker URL and keeps only its host and port, so credentials in the URL never reach the document, which is published. protocol_version names the version clients speak, where one protocol name covers incompatible versions, as AMQP 0.9.1 and 1.0 do. description adds a note for the reader. A server spec holds coordinates, never configuration. How clients authenticate is security, and what the protocol adds is bindings. The example runs with cargo test --example asyncapi_servers --features macros,memory,asyncapi.

examples/asyncapi_servers.rs /// The cluster the service is deployed against, as its clients reach it. fn production() -> ServerSpec { ServerSpec::new("kafka.example.com:9093", "kafka") .protocol_version("3.9") .description("The production cluster") } Macros Manual examples/asyncapi_servers.rs fn app() -> Result<impl App, BindingError> { let production = with_registry(secured(production()))?; Ok(RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) // Declared: no broker of this process describes the cluster. .server("production", production) // Described by the broker itself, under its label. .with_broker_labeled("in-process", MemoryBroker::new(), |b| b.include(accept))) } examples/manual/asyncapi_servers.rs fn app() -> Result<impl App, BindingError> { let production = with_registry(secured(production()))?; Ok(RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) // Declared: no broker of this process describes the cluster. .server("production", production) // Described by the broker itself, under its label. .with_broker_labeled("in-process", MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Accept).build()) })) }

with_broker_labeled registers a broker under a label that is its server name in the document, and the broker describes the server. with_broker_labeled takes a broker that implements DescribeServer; every shipped broker does. The broker fills the server entry in its protocol's vocabulary: host, protocol, protocol version and bindings. The in-memory broker describes an in-process server over the memory protocol, with no host. The label is also the broker's identity in the service; a test addresses the broker by it with broker_named. The registration's channels list the server, and its operations carry the server's protocol as a tag, so a document with several brokers reads by transport. A document with one server puts every channel on it. With several, the channels of an unlabeled registration list none, which AsyncAPI reads as "on every server". An explicit server under the same label takes precedence over what the broker says. with_broker_labeled_codec also names the scope's codec. The example runs with cargo test --example asyncapi_servers --features macros,memory,asyncapi.

Macros Manual examples/asyncapi_servers.rs fn app() -> Result<impl App, BindingError> { let production = with_registry(secured(production()))?; Ok(RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) // Declared: no broker of this process describes the cluster. .server("production", production) // Described by the broker itself, under its label. .with_broker_labeled("in-process", MemoryBroker::new(), |b| b.include(accept))) } examples/manual/asyncapi_servers.rs fn app() -> Result<impl App, BindingError> { let production = with_registry(secured(production()))?; Ok(RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) // Declared: no broker of this process describes the cluster. .server("production", production) // Described by the broker itself, under its label. .with_broker_labeled("in-process", MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Accept).build()) })) }
The info section: what the service is, who owns it and under which license. It comes from the AppInfo the app is built with, and the service's id sits at the root of the document.

AppId is the identifier of the service at the root of the document, a URI parsed when it is built. AsyncAPI requires the id to be a URI. AppId checks the part a URI scheme must have: a letter, then letters, digits, +, - or ., then a colon. What follows the colon is the scheme's business. A bare title fails with AppIdError::NoScheme, and a malformed scheme with MalformedScheme. AppInfo::id sets it, and only a parsed AppId fits there. An id from the deployment's configuration therefore fails where the app is built, never in a published document. The example runs with cargo test --example asyncapi_info --no-default-features --features asyncapi.

examples/asyncapi_info.rs /// The id comes from the deployment's configuration, so a value that is not a URI stops the /// build of the app. fn app(id: &str) -> Result<impl App, AppIdError> { let id: AppId = id.parse()?; Ok(RustStream::new(info().id(id))) }

AppInfo is the info section of the document: the title and the version, a description and the terms of service. AppInfo::new takes the title and the version, which every document carries. description and terms_of_service fill two optional fields. The contact, the license, the tags and the external docs are pages of their own. A field left empty is left out of the document. The app is built from the same AppInfo, so the service's logs and its document name it the same way. The example runs with cargo test --example asyncapi_info --no-default-features --features asyncapi.

examples/asyncapi_info.rs /// What the service is, who owns it, and under what terms it runs. fn info() -> AppInfo { AppInfo::new("payments", "1.4.0") .description("Everything the payment domain publishes.") .terms_of_service("https://example.com/terms") .contact(contact()) .license(license()) .tag(tag()) .external_docs(external_docs()) }

Contact names who answers for the service: a person or a team, a URL and an e-mail address, each optional. AppInfo::contact sets it. Contact::new starts empty, and name, url and email fill the fields. A contact with no field filled is left out of the document. The example runs with cargo test --example asyncapi_info --no-default-features --features asyncapi.

examples/asyncapi_info.rs /// Who answers for the service; every field is optional. fn contact() -> Contact { Contact::new() .name("Payments team") .url("https://example.com/teams/payments") .email("payments@example.com") }

ExternalDocs points at documentation kept outside the document: a URL and what the reader finds there. AppInfo::external_docs sets it for the service, and Tag::external_docs for a tag. ExternalDocs::new takes the URL. description says what is there. The example runs with cargo test --example asyncapi_info --no-default-features --features asyncapi.
examples/asyncapi_info.rs /// Where the prose about the service lives. fn external_docs() -> ExternalDocs { ExternalDocs::new("https://example.com/runbooks/payments").description("The runbook") }

License names the license the service is published under, with an optional URL of its text. AppInfo::license sets it. License::new takes the name, an SPDX identifier by convention. url points at the license text. The example runs with cargo test --example asyncapi_info --no-default-features --features asyncapi.
examples/asyncapi_info.rs /// The license, by its SPDX identifier and where its text is. fn license() -> License { License::new("Apache-2.0").url("https://spdx.org/licenses/Apache-2.0.html") }

A Tag is a label that groups the service among its neighbours, with an optional description and link. AppInfo::tag adds one; each call adds another. Tag::new takes the label. description says what it means, and external_docs where it is documented. The document also tags each operation with the protocol of its server. The example runs with cargo test --example asyncapi_info --no-default-features --features asyncapi.

examples/asyncapi_info.rs /// The domain the service belongs to among its neighbours. fn tag() -> Tag { Tag::new("payments") .description("Everything that moves money") .external_docs(ExternalDocs::new("https://example.com/domains/payments")) }

MemoryBroker is a complete broker inside the service's process, and the reference implementation of the broker contract. It comes with the memory feature and needs no server. It suits a queue that belongs to one process, a prototype, or local development; the default cargo generate template starts on it. MemoryBroker::new does no I/O, like every broker constructor. A broker built with it keeps nothing: a message lives until the last subscriber has read it, so memory holds the work the handlers have yet to do. A broker that keeps the newest messages for replay is built with retaining. A mount site imports ruststream::memory::prelude, one glob with the core prelude, the broker's own types, and its publish policies under the names every broker crate uses: Publish, TransactionalPublish and Request. Partitioned stays out of the glob, because in scope it makes msg.partition_key() ambiguous; a service that reads partition keys imports it. A handler body that names capabilities, not policies, keeps ruststream::prelude::*. A subscription by name reads messages published to that exact name, from the moment it opens. Every subscription of a name receives every message published to it. MemorySource is the broker's subscription descriptor, and MemoryPattern reads every name a pattern matches. An ack or a drop consumes a delivery; a retry, or a delivery left without a settlement, comes back to the same subscriber. A retry_after delivery comes back to the same subscriber after its delay, and nothing is republished. Every delivery reports how many times the broker has handed it to that subscriber, so a registration's attempt cap counts these redeliveries. MemoryBroker is a shared handle: its clones work on one bus. After shutdown, a publish, a commit or a request through a handle taken earlier returns an error.

The dependency line: ruststream = { version = "0.8", features = ["macros", "memory", "json"] } Two subscriptions to orders each receive the order, and one of them replies over the same bus. Macros Manual examples/memory_broker.rs use ruststream::memory::prelude::*; #[subscriber("orders", reply("confirmations"))] async fn confirm(order: &Order) -> Confirmation { Confirmation { id: order.id } } #[subscriber("orders")] async fn audit(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "audited"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| b.include(confirm).include(audit)) } examples/manual/memory_broker.rs use ruststream::memory::prelude::*; struct Confirm; impl Handle<Order, Confirmation> for Confirm { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Confirmation, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(Confirmation { id: order.id })) } } struct Audit; impl Handle<Order> for Audit { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "audited"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include( subscriber("orders", Confirm) .reply() .to("confirmations") .build(), ) .include(subscriber("orders", Audit).build()) }) }

The broker implements the optional capabilities on its own in-process semantics. Request and reply: broker.requester() gives a MemoryRequester, which names a unique reply name in the reply-to header and waits for the first message delivered there. Request is its policy. Batches: a batch is the first delivery to arrive plus everything already buffered, up to the size the registration names. Transactions: the publisher behind Publish implements TransactionalPublisher and OwnedTransactions. A commit delivers the buffered messages at once, in publish order; an abort discards them. Partition keys: a MemoryMessage reads its key from the partition-key header. Replay: on a retaining broker, a subscription opens at a start position and a handler seeks. The TestApp harness runs an application on this broker as it runs one on a networked broker, and its publishes wait on exactly the subscriptions the broker's routing picks.

A MemoryPattern subscription reads every name its pattern matches, and the broker's Routing decides who receives a shared match. Patterns use the NATS subject syntax. A name splits into tokens at .. * matches exactly one token, and > as the last token matches one or more. So orders.* reads orders.eu and orders.us, and orders.> also reads orders.eu.created. The broker checks a pattern when the subscription opens; a bad one stops the service at startup with MemoryError::InvalidPattern, which names it. A subscription by name reads one name, and a wildcard token in it stops the service with MemoryError::WildcardName. MemoryBroker::routing sets the rule for a publish that several subscriptions match. Routing::EveryMatch, the default, delivers it to every match, as NATS does: a pattern reads beside the handlers of single names, as an audit trail or a metrics tap. Routing::MostSpecific delivers it to the subscriptions of the exact name, or, where there are none, to the most specific matching pattern: a pattern is the fallback for names without a handler of their own. Patterns are compared token by token from the left, and at the first difference a literal beats *, and * beats >. For orders.eu.created, orders.eu.* beats orders.*.created, which beats orders.>, which beats *.eu.created. A broker with no pattern subscription routes by the exact name alone and pays nothing for patterns. A pattern subscription does not replay, even on a retaining broker.

orders.eu goes to its own handler alone, and the pattern takes every other region. Macros Manual examples/memory_patterns.rs #[subscriber("orders.eu")] async fn europe(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "european order"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// Reads every `orders.<region>` name. #[subscriber(MemoryPattern::new("orders.*"))] async fn other_regions(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order from another region"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { // `orders.eu` goes to `europe` alone; the pattern takes the names nobody else reads. let broker = MemoryBroker::new().routing(Routing::MostSpecific); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(broker, |b| b.include(europe).include(other_regions)) } examples/manual/memory_patterns.rs struct Europe; impl Handle<Order> for Europe { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "european order"); ready(Ok(())) } } struct OtherRegions; impl Handle<Order> for OtherRegions { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order from another region"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { // `orders.eu` goes to `Europe` alone; the pattern takes the names nobody else reads. let broker = MemoryBroker::new().routing(Routing::MostSpecific); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders.eu", Europe).build()) // Reads every `orders.<region>` name. .include(subscriber(MemoryPattern::new("orders.*"), OtherRegions).build()) }) }

A retaining MemoryBroker keeps the newest messages of every name within a bound, and its subscriptions replay over them. MemoryBroker::retaining takes a Retention bound, applied to each name on its own. Retention::Messages(n) keeps the newest n messages. Retention::Bytes(n) keeps the newest payloads that fit in n bytes. Retention::MessagesAndBytes { .. } applies both. A broker that publishes under a thousand names keeps up to that much for each of them. The newest message always stays, so a payload larger than a byte bound is kept alone. The retaining broker is a type of its own, MemoryBroker<Retaining>, and only its subscriptions implement Seekable. A start_at or a seek therefore does not compile on MemoryBroker::new(), which keeps nothing. A MemoryPosition names a place in the log of one name: start() is the oldest message still kept, sequence(n) the n-th message ever published to the name, and end() the tip. A sequence number keeps naming the same message as the bound evicts older ones. A sequence the bound has already evicted is refused with MemoryError::PositionEvicted, which names the oldest position left. A pattern subscription does not replay, because the log is kept per name.

The broker keeps two messages of each name; three published before the service starts leave the last two to replay. Macros Manual examples/memory_retention.rs /// Keeps the newest two messages of every name. fn broker() -> MemoryBroker<Retaining> { MemoryBroker::retaining(Retention::Messages(nonzero!(2))) } /// Opens at the oldest message still kept, so it reads what came before the service. #[subscriber("audit", start_at(MemoryPosition::start()))] async fn record(entry: &Entry) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(entry.id, "recorded"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn app(broker: MemoryBroker<Retaining>) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("audit", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| b.include(record)) } examples/manual/memory_retention.rs /// Keeps the newest two messages of every name. fn broker() -> MemoryBroker<Retaining> { MemoryBroker::retaining(Retention::Messages(nonzero!(2))) } struct Record; impl Handle<Entry> for Record { fn handle( &self, entry: &Entry, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(entry.id, "recorded"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app(broker: MemoryBroker<Retaining>) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("audit", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // Opens at the oldest message still kept, so it reads what came before the service. b.include( subscriber("audit", Record) .start_at(MemoryPosition::start()) .build(), ) }) }

Logs, metrics and traces of a running service: each comes from a layer on the app and a feature that exports it. RustStream reports what it does through tracing events, and the logging feature prints them on the console. The per-delivery signals come from layers that wrap every handler, so a handler body holds only its own logic. A layer added to the app wraps the handlers of its routers too. Prometheus metrics need the metrics feature; trace propagation and OpenTelemetry export need the otel feature.

The logging feature prints the service's tracing events on the console, colored, at the verbosity RUST_LOG sets. RustStream emits tracing events while it dispatches, publishes and starts or stops the service, and a handler emits its own with tracing::info! and its siblings. Nothing is printed until a tracing subscriber is installed. logging::init installs the bundled one. It writes to stderr, so stdout stays clean for the output of a command such as asyncapi gen. Levels are colored when stderr is a terminal. RUST_LOG sets the filter in the usual directive syntax; without it, the filter is info. The main that #[ruststream::app] generates calls init on run, so a service with the attribute needs no setup. A hand-written main calls init itself, or builds a Logging to change the defaults: the fallback filter, colors, and whether each line names its target. try_init installs it, and returns LoggingInitError when the filter does not parse or a subscriber is already installed. A subscriber installed first stays in place: the generated main leaves a service's own stack alone, a JSON formatter or an OpenTelemetry bridge for one. The events of each delivery and its outcome come from TracingLayer.

The example runs with the logger on: RUST_LOG=ruststream=debug,info cargo run --example logging --features testing,macros,memory,json,logging -- run Macros Manual examples/logging.rs #[subscriber("orders")] async fn accept(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "order accepted"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| b.include(accept)) } examples/manual/logging.rs struct Accept; impl Handle<Order> for Accept { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "order accepted"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Accept).build()) }) } fn main() -> Result<ExitCode, LoggingInitError> { // `RUST_LOG` still wins; this filter applies when it is unset. Logging::new() .with_default_filter("ruststream=debug,info") .try_init()?; // `run_main` finds the logger installed and leaves it in place. Ok(run_main(app)) }

The metrics feature counts and times deliveries and counts publishes in a Prometheus registry that the service serves on /metrics. A Metrics value owns the collectors and the registry they are registered in. Metrics::new registers them in the process's default registry, so a process builds one. Metrics::with_registry registers them in a registry of your own, and registry hands the registry out for collectors of your own. consume_layer is a layer for the app: it times every handler and counts its outcome. publish_layer is a publish layer: it counts every publish a handler makes, replies included, and the failed ones too. Metrics is cheap to clone, and every clone writes into the same collectors. Metric Type Labels ruststream_messages_consumed_total counter name, status: ack or nack ruststream_consume_duration_seconds histogram name ruststream_messages_published_total counter name, status: ok or error name is the subscription on the consume side and the destination on the publish side. With the poll-diagnostics feature, observe_poll_diagnostics adds the time handlers spend in one poll, as described in Diagnostics. export renders the registry in the Prometheus text format. Serving it is the service's part: a route of its HTTP server, or a push to a gateway.

The example serves /metrics on port 8080: cargo run --example metrics --features testing,macros,memory,json,metrics Macros Manual examples/metrics.rs #[subscriber("orders", reply("confirmations"))] async fn confirm(order: &Order) -> Confirmation { Confirmation { id: order.id, accepted: order.quantity > 0, } } fn app(metrics: &Metrics, broker: MemoryBroker) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) // Counts and times every delivery, by subscription and outcome. .layer(metrics.consume_layer()) // Counts every publish, the replies included, by destination and outcome. .publish_layer(metrics.publish_layer()) .with_broker(broker, |b| b.include(confirm)) } examples/manual/metrics.rs struct Confirm; impl Handle<Order, Confirmation> for Confirm { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Confirmation, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(Confirmation { id: order.id, accepted: order.quantity > 0, })) } } fn app(metrics: &Metrics, broker: MemoryBroker) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) // Counts and times every delivery, by subscription and outcome. .layer(metrics.consume_layer()) // Counts every publish, the replies included, by destination and outcome. .publish_layer(metrics.publish_layer()) .with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include( subscriber("orders", Confirm) .reply() .to("confirmations") .build(), ) }) } The route that serves the registry is an ordinary axum handler. examples/metrics.rs /// The `/metrics` route: the registry in the Prometheus text format. async fn scrape(State(metrics): State<Metrics>) -> Result<String, StatusCode> { metrics .export() .map_err(|_| StatusCode::INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR) }

Otel sends the service's spans and metrics to an OpenTelemetry collector over OTLP, the dispatch metrics included. Otel::builder starts an OtelBuilder. It takes the service.name, the OTLP endpoint, the messaging.system the dispatch metrics carry, and extra resource attributes such as the environment. An endpoint left unset comes from the standard OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_* environment, http://localhost:4317 by default. init builds the exporters and installs the tracer and meter providers as the process's globals. It also installs a tracing subscriber that bridges spans into the tracer, so the spans of Propagation are exported with no further wiring. A service with a subscriber of its own turns the bridge off with tracing_bridge(false) and adds it to its own stack. consume_layer and publish_layer record the dispatch metrics, named by the messaging semantic conventions and labelled per subscription or destination: Instrument What it measures messaging.client.consumed.messages deliveries received messaging.process.duration handler time ruststream.messages.processed settlements, by outcome: ack, nack_requeue, nack_drop, retry_after ruststream.messages.in_flight deliveries inside handlers ruststream.message.queue_time time from publish to handler, from the publish-time header the publish layer stamps ruststream.messages.decode_failures, ruststream.messages.panics payloads the codec rejected, handlers that panicked messaging.client.sent.messages, messaging.client.operation.duration publishes and their time ruststream.message.payload.size published payload sizes ruststream.batch.size decoded batch sizes, recorded by batch dispatch once init has run The duration histograms use the buckets the conventions advise, 5 ms to 10 s; view changes them per instrument. observe_health adds the ruststream.app.state gauge over the app's health probe. The service's own instruments come from opentelemetry::global::meter and go out through the same pipeline; the example builds them once at startup and shares them as state. Spans and metric points are batched in the background. shutdown flushes them, after the app has stopped; dropping Otel does not. A hand-written main makes that call, which is why the example keeps one with and without the macros. attach takes providers built by the caller and installs no globals: an exporter of your own, or an in-memory one in a test. A Grafana dashboard over these instruments is in ruststream-grafana.

The example exports to a collector on localhost:4317; without one, the exporter retries in the background and the service keeps working: cargo run --example otel_export --features testing,macros,memory,json,otel -- run main installs the exporters, runs the app, and flushes at the end. examples/otel_export.rs // Written by hand rather than by `#[ruststream::app]`: the exporters batch in the background, // so `main` flushes them once the app has drained. fn main() -> Result<ExitCode, Box<dyn Error>> { let otel = Otel::builder() .service_name("orders") .otlp_endpoint("http://localhost:4317") .messaging_system("memory") .attribute("deployment.environment", "dev") .init()?; let code = run_main(|| app(&otel)); // Ships the last spans and metric points; dropping `Otel` does not. otel.shutdown()?; Ok(code) } The app takes both layers and builds the service's own instrument at startup. Macros Manual examples/otel_export.rs // `use<>`: the app keeps its own handles to the instruments, not a borrow of `otel`. fn app(otel: &Otel) -> impl App + use<> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) // Per delivery: consumed, processing time, outcomes, in flight, queue time. .layer(otel.consume_layer()) // Per publish: sent, operation time, payload size, the publish-time stamp. .publish_layer(otel.publish_layer()) .on_startup(async move |()| { Ok::<_, Infallible>(AppState { metrics: OrderMetrics { accepted: global::meter("orders") .u64_counter("orders_accepted") .build(), }, }) }) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| b.include(accept)) } examples/manual/otel_export.rs // `use<>`: the app keeps its own handles to the instruments, not a borrow of `otel`. fn app(otel: &Otel) -> impl App + use<> { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) // Per delivery: consumed, processing time, outcomes, in flight, queue time. .layer(otel.consume_layer()) // Per publish: sent, operation time, payload size, the publish-time stamp. .publish_layer(otel.publish_layer()) .on_startup(async move |()| { Ok::<_, Infallible>(AppState { metrics: OrderMetrics { accepted: global::meter("orders") .u64_counter("orders_accepted") .build(), }, }) }) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Accept).build()) }) } The handler records the instrument it reads from the state. Macros Manual examples/otel_export.rs /// The service's own instruments, built once at startup against the global meter, so they /// export through the same pipeline as the dispatch metrics. #[derive(Clone)] struct OrderMetrics { accepted: Counter<u64>, } #[derive(Clone, FromRef)] struct AppState { metrics: OrderMetrics, } #[subscriber("orders")] async fn accept(_order: &Order, State(metrics): State<OrderMetrics>) -> HandlerOutcome { metrics.accepted.add(1, &[KeyValue::new("region", "eu")]); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/otel_export.rs /// The service's own instruments, built once at startup against the global meter, so they /// export through the same pipeline as the dispatch metrics. #[derive(Clone)] struct OrderMetrics { accepted: Counter<u64>, } // A hand-written handler reads the state whole off the context, so it needs no `FromRef`. #[derive(Clone)] struct AppState { metrics: OrderMetrics, } struct Accept; // The state is the last axis of `Handle`; the mount checks it against the app's. impl Handle<Order, (), (), (), AppState> for Accept { fn handle( &self, _order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), AppState>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { ctx.state() .metrics .accepted .add(1, &[KeyValue::new("region", "eu")]); ready(Ok(())) } }

The otel feature carries the W3C trace context from a delivery to its replies and opens a span for every delivery. OpenTelemetry hands out two pieces. consume_layer is a layer for the app. For each delivery it reads the traceparent and tracestate headers and continues that trace with a new span id: the consumer's span. A delivery without a valid traceparent starts a new sampled trace. The handler runs inside an INFO span named ruststream.consume, which records the subscription and both ids. The layer writes the consumer's context into the delivery's working headers, where a handler reads it: ctx.headers().get_str("traceparent"). propagation is a publish transform for a reply position. It copies traceparent and tracestate from the working headers onto every reply, so the next service continues the same trace with the consumer span as the parent. for_batch(otel.propagation()) puts it on a batch reply. The headers are parsed and written by the OpenTelemetry SDK's W3C propagator, which follows the specification strictly. Propagation works with any tracing subscriber, or none; Export sends the spans to a collector.

Macros Manual examples/otel_propagation.rs #[subscriber("orders", reply("confirmations"))] async fn confirm(order: &Order) -> Confirmation { Confirmation { id: order.id } } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { let otel = OpenTelemetry::new(); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) // A span per delivery, a child of the trace the delivery carries. .layer(otel.consume_layer()) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { // The reply carries the consumer span's trace context. b.include(confirm) .out_reply(Publish) .transform(otel.propagation()) }) } examples/manual/otel_propagation.rs struct Confirm; impl Handle<Order, Confirmation> for Confirm { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Confirmation, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(Confirmation { id: order.id })) } } fn app() -> impl App { let otel = OpenTelemetry::new(); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) // A span per delivery, a child of the trace the delivery carries. .layer(otel.consume_layer()) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { // The reply carries the consumer span's trace context. b.include( subscriber("orders", Confirm) .reply() .to("confirmations") .build(), ) .out_reply(Publish) .transform(otel.propagation()) }) }

TracingLayer logs every delivery and its outcome as tracing events, so handlers hold no logging code of their own. It is a layer bundled with the runtime. Added to the app with RustStream::layer, it wraps every handler, those of routers included. Each delivery gives a DEBUG event when it reaches the handler and one more event when the handler settles it. An ack is logged at INFO. A nack is logged at WARN with requeue=true or requeue=false, and a delayed retry at WARN with its delay. The events go under the ruststream::dispatch target, so RUST_LOG=ruststream::dispatch=debug shows them alone. The handler runs inside a TRACE span; TracingLayer::with_target records a name on that span. The layer never changes the outcome it logs. The events need a tracing subscriber to show, such as the one Logging installs. Batch handlers are not wrapped by app layers, so their deliveries are not logged here.

The handler acks an order and drops an empty one; the layer logs both outcomes. Macros Manual examples/tracing_layer.rs #[subscriber("orders")] async fn confirm(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { if order.quantity == 0 { // The layer logs this outcome as a WARN with `requeue=false`. return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) // Wraps every handler the app mounts, router handlers included. .layer(TracingLayer::default()) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| b.include(confirm)) } examples/manual/tracing_layer.rs struct Confirm; impl Handle<Order> for Confirm { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { if order.quantity == 0 { // The layer logs this outcome as a WARN with `requeue=false`. return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::drop())); } ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) // Wraps every handler the app mounts, router handlers included. .layer(TracingLayer::default()) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Confirm).build()) }) }

#[subscriber] turns an async fn over a reference to the message into a handler that include mounts on a broker. The first parameter is the message: &T handles one message, &[T] a whole batch. The runtime decodes the payload with the scope's codec before the body runs; a serde type is all the input needs. A subscription that carries several message types takes an enum that derives InMessages, one model per variant: the message sets page. A payload that does not decode never reaches the body: the decode failure policy settles it, and drops it by default. An optional &mut Context comes second, and any further parameter is an extractor resolved before the body runs: the context page covers both. What the body returns settles the delivery: HandlerOutcome, () (ack), Result<(), E> (ack on Ok, drop on Err) or Result<HandlerOutcome, E>, as the outcomes page shows. The attribute expands into a definition value named after the function, and include on a broker scope of the application or a router mounts it. The attribute's first argument is the subscription source; settings it leaves out are chained at the mount site. The manual form writes the body as an impl Handle<T> of a named type, binds it with subscriber(source, body) and closes the chain with .build(). There Ok(()) acks and Err(outcome) settles by that outcome.

Macros Manual examples/subscriber_handler.rs #[subscriber("orders")] async fn accept(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "accepted"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| b.include(accept)) } examples/manual/subscriber_handler.rs struct Accept; impl Handle<Order> for Accept { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "accepted"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Accept).build()) }) }

A handler over &[T] runs once per batch the broker delivers; the mount site names the batch size, and the body settles the batch or each element. The slice parameter is the whole declaration: a &[T] handler is a batch handler, and a &T handler is the single-message form of #[subscriber]. batch(n), one of the mount-site settings, caps each batch at n messages, and a batch handler does not mount without it. The broker builds the batches, natively or through the framework's client-side buffer, and the body sees each batch as delivered. A batch may hold fewer than n messages. The batch's return value settles every element with one of the outcomes: HandlerOutcome, (), Result<(), E> or Result<HandlerOutcome, E>. A Vec<HandlerOutcome> settles each element on its own, retry_after included; a vector of the wrong length is logged, and the elements it leaves unsettled are retried. An element that fails to decode is settled by the decode failure policy and never reaches the body. The body gets one context per batch, with the broker's subscription-scoped fields only. Per-message headers come with the elements when the parameter is &[Message<H, T>]. App-wide and router middleware wrap single-message handlers and do not apply to batch handlers. In the manual form the body is an impl Handle<[T]>; Ok(()) acks the batch and Err(outcomes) settles element by element. A test reads the batches with batches and checks their sizes with assert_batch_sizes.

One outcome settles the whole batch. Macros Manual examples/subscriber_batch.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "orders")] struct Order { id: u64, } /// One call per batch; the one outcome settles every order in it. #[subscriber("orders")] async fn store(orders: &[Order]) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(count = orders.len(), "stored in one round-trip"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn app(broker: MemoryBroker) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // At most 64 orders per call. b.include(store.batch(nonzero!(64))) }) } examples/manual/subscriber_batch.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, schemars::JsonSchema)] struct Order { id: u64, } // `#[outgoing(name = "orders")]` by hand: the type fixes its destination. impl OutgoingDestination for Order { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "orders"; } impl MessageHeaders for Order { type Contract = NoHeaders; } /// One call per batch; `Ok` settles every order in it. struct Store; impl Handle<[Order]> for Store { fn handle( &self, orders: &[Order], _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), Vec<HandlerOutcome>>> { tracing::info!(count = orders.len(), "stored in one round-trip"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn app(broker: MemoryBroker) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // At most 64 orders per call. b.include(subscriber("orders", Store).batch(nonzero!(64)).build()) }) }

A Vec<HandlerOutcome> settles element i with outcome i. Macros Manual examples/subscriber_batch.rs const RECHECK: Duration = Duration::from_secs(30); #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "payments")] struct Payment { id: u64, cleared: bool, } /// One outcome per element, in slice order: only the uncleared payments come back. #[subscriber("payments")] async fn reconcile(payments: &[Payment]) -> Vec<HandlerOutcome> { payments .iter() .map(|payment| { if payment.cleared { HandlerOutcome::ack() } else { HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RECHECK) } }) .collect() } examples/manual/subscriber_batch.rs const RECHECK: Duration = Duration::from_secs(30); #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, schemars::JsonSchema)] struct Payment { id: u64, cleared: bool, } // `#[outgoing(name = "payments")]` by hand: the type fixes its destination. impl OutgoingDestination for Payment { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "payments"; } impl MessageHeaders for Payment { type Contract = NoHeaders; } /// One outcome per element, in slice order: only the uncleared payments come back. struct Reconcile; impl Handle<[Payment]> for Reconcile { fn handle( &self, payments: &[Payment], _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), Vec<HandlerOutcome>>> { ready(Err(payments .iter() .map(|payment| { if payment.cleared { HandlerOutcome::ack() } else { HandlerOutcome::retry_after(RECHECK) } }) .collect())) } } fn app(broker: MemoryBroker) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include( subscriber("payments", Reconcile) .batch(nonzero!(64)) .build(), ) }) }

A codec turns a payload into a message type and back; it is a compile-time type, chosen at the mount site, and JSON is the default. A Codec decodes the bytes of a delivery into the type the handler reads, and encodes what the handler publishes. It belongs to the mounting, not to the message type, so one type can arrive in JSON on one subscription and in CBOR on another. The codec is resolved when the app is built, so choosing one costs nothing per message. A handler decodes with the codec of the most specific level that names one: Level Macros Manual registration Router::new().with_codec(codec).include(def) subscriber(..).codec(codec) scope with_broker_codec(broker, codec, |b| ..) the same default DefaultCodec the same with_broker_codec names the codec for every handler of a broker scope. A router names one for the handlers it mounts with Router::with_codec. DefaultCodec is the first enabled of the json, cbor and msgpack features, in that order. With no codec feature, a mounting that needs the default does not compile, and the error lists the ways out. The publish side names its codec at its own position. A reply takes the default codec unless .out_reply(policy).codec(codec) names another, so a request and its reply may use different formats. An Out slot takes .out(marker, policy).codec(codec); without it a slot encodes with the codec of the router or scope it is mounted in, not the default codec a reply falls back to. A single publish takes .with_codec(codec) on the builder. A payload that does not decode never reaches the body. The subscriber's on_failure(decode = ..) policy settles it, a drop by default. A type that carries its own bytes skips the codec: Protobuf and the byte lanes need no codec feature.

Macros Manual examples/codecs.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("codecs", "0.1.0")).with_broker_codec( MemoryBroker::new(), // Every handler of this scope decodes CBOR. CborCodec, |b| { // A router names the codec of the handlers it mounts. b.include_router(Router::new().with_codec(JsonCodec).include(audit)) .include(bill) // A reply takes the default codec, JSON, unless its position names one. .include(checkout) .out_reply(Publish) .codec(CborCodec) }, ) } examples/manual/codecs.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("codecs", "0.1.0")).with_broker_codec( MemoryBroker::new(), // Every registration of this scope decodes CBOR. CborCodec, |b| { b.include(subscriber("orders", Bill).build()) // A registration names its own codec. .include(subscriber("audit", Audit).codec(JsonCodec).build()) // A reply takes the default codec, JSON, unless its position names one. .include( subscriber("checkout", Checkout) .reply() .to("receipts") .build(), ) .out_reply(Publish) .codec(CborCodec) }, ) }

A handler that reads the delivery's bytes as they arrived, and a reply that leaves as the bytes it holds, skip the codec. A newtype over &'a [u8] deriving Deserialized is a view of the payload, borrowed from the broker's buffer. A handler over &Frame<'_> receives it with no copy and no decode step, and &[Frame<'_>] is the batch form. A bare &[u8] parameter does not compile: the newtype names what the bytes are. A newtype over Vec<u8> deriving Serialized publishes its bytes as they are, as a reply, an Out slot or a publish from the builder. The two lanes mix freely with codecs: a handler can decode its input with the scope codec and reply in bytes, or the other way round. A service whose messages are all on the lanes builds with no codec feature. A type that holds fields and writes its own format uses the same derives with #[wire(..)], as Protobuf does. In the manual form the impls the derives write are spelled out.

The example builds with no codec feature: cargo test --example byte_lanes --no-default-features --features testing,macros,memory Macros Manual examples/byte_lanes.rs /// The delivery's bytes, borrowed from the broker's buffer. #[derive(Deserialized)] struct Frame<'a>(&'a [u8]); /// Bytes that leave as they are. #[derive(Outgoing, Serialized)] struct Export(Vec<u8>); #[subscriber("frames", reply("exports"))] async fn reverse(frame: &Frame<'_>) -> Export { tracing::info!(len = frame.0.len(), "reversed"); let mut bytes = frame.0.to_vec(); bytes.reverse(); Export(bytes) } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("frames", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| b.include(reverse)) } examples/manual/byte_lanes.rs /// The delivery's bytes, borrowed from the broker's buffer. struct Frame<'a>(&'a [u8]); // `#[derive(Deserialized)]` by hand: the view borrows the payload, and `&Frame<'_>` takes the // lane that reads no codec. impl Deserialized for Frame<'_> { type Output<'a> = Frame<'a>; type Error = Infallible; fn from_payload(payload: &[u8]) -> Result<Frame<'_>, Self::Error> { Ok(Frame(payload)) } } impl Input for Frame<'_> { type Axis = SoloDeserialized<Frame<'static>>; } /// Bytes that leave as they are. struct Export(Vec<u8>); // `#[derive(Serialized)]` by hand: the bytes, the wire of a typed publish, the shape of a reply. impl Serialized for Export { type Error = Infallible; fn wire_bytes(&self, _buf: &mut BytesMut) -> Result<WireBytes<'_>, Infallible> { Ok(WireBytes::Own(&self.0)) } } impl MessageWire for Export { type Wire = SerializedWire; } impl ReplyShape for Export { type Body = Self; type Headers = (); type Wire = SerializedReply; } // `#[derive(Outgoing)]` with no `name`, by hand: the call site names the destination. impl OutgoingDestination for Export { type Form = CallerName; } impl MessageHeaders for Export { type Contract = NoHeaders; } struct Reverse; impl<'p> Handle<Frame<'p>, Export> for Reverse { fn handle( &self, frame: &Frame<'p>, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Export, HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(len = frame.0.len(), "reversed"); let mut bytes = frame.0.to_vec(); bytes.reverse(); ready(Ok(Export(bytes))) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("frames", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("frames", Reverse).reply().to("exports").build()) }) }

CborCodec reads and writes CBOR through ciborium, a compact binary format with the data model of JSON; it is on with the cbor feature. A message type derives the same serde traits as for JSON, and a struct keeps its field names on the wire. The media type is application/cbor. The example names the codec on the scope with with_broker_codec, so it holds whichever other codec features are on. With cbor as the only codec feature, DefaultCodec is CborCodec, and a mounting needs to name nothing. A payload in another format is a decode failure, settled by the subscriber's failure policy.
