Macros Manual examples/destinations.rs #[subscriber("orders.incoming")] async fn route(order: &Order, Out(orders): Out<impl Publisher, Orders>) -> HandlerOutcome { let confirmed = orders .message(&OrderConfirmed { id: order.id }) .publish() .await; let placed = orders .message(&OrderPlaced { id: order.id }) .to() .tenant(&order.tenant) .publish() .await; let notice = orders .message(&Notice { id: order.id }) .to("notices") .publish() .await; if confirmed.is_err() || placed.is_err() || notice.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/destinations.rs struct Route; impl<O> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(O,)>> for Route where O: OutEntry<Orders, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(O,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let orders = outs.get(Orders); let confirmed = orders .message(&OrderConfirmed { id: order.id }) .publish() .await; let placed = orders .message(&OrderPlaced { id: order.id }) .to() .tenant(&order.tenant) .publish() .await; let notice = orders .message(&Notice { id: order.id }) .to("notices") .publish() .await; if confirmed.is_err() || placed.is_err() || notice.is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(()) } }

One builder publishes every message: message(&value), the positions its type leaves open, then publish(). A slot, a transaction and any bare Publisher start a publish with message(&value) and return a PublishBuilder. The positions the message type leaves open come next. .to(name) names the destination of a type that declares none, and a template opens .to() with its setters, as on the Destinations page. A publish whose destination is still open does not compile. .with_headers(..) takes the type's declared header contract by reference, or a HeaderMap built by hand. The headers on the wire are the publisher's base headers with the call site's over them, key by key. .with_codec(codec) names a codec for this one publish, over the slot's and the app's. A Serialized value carries its own bytes and has no codec position. A broker adds steps of its own for its per-message settings. publish() encodes the value and sends it, and returns PublishError on failure. Encode and Serialize mean the value did not encode, and a retry of the same value fails the same way. Publish carries the broker's own error. On a slot the message passes the slot's transforms before the send, and the app's publish layers where they apply.

Macros Manual examples/publish_builder.rs #[subscriber("shipments")] async fn notify(shipment: &Shipment, Out(out): Out<impl Publisher>) -> HandlerOutcome { let mut headers = HeaderMap::new(); headers.insert("carrier", shipment.carrier.clone()); let sent = out .message(&Notice { id: shipment.id }) .to(format!("notices.{}", shipment.region)) .with_headers(headers) .publish() .await; match sent { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), // A value that does not encode fails the same way on every attempt. Err(PublishError::Encode(_) | PublishError::Serialize(_)) => HandlerOutcome::drop(), Err(_) => HandlerOutcome::retry(), } } examples/manual/publish_builder.rs struct Notify; impl<Egress> Handle<Shipment, (), Outs<(Egress,)>> for Notify where Egress: OutEntry<DefaultSlot, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, shipment: &Shipment, outs: &Outs<(Egress,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let mut headers = HeaderMap::new(); headers.insert("carrier", shipment.carrier.clone()); let sent = outs .get(DefaultSlot) .message(&Notice { id: shipment.id }) .to(format!("notices.{}", shipment.region)) .with_headers(headers) .publish() .await; match sent { Ok(()) => Ok(()), // A value that does not encode fails the same way on every attempt. Err(PublishError::Encode(_) | PublishError::Serialize(_)) => { Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()) } Err(_) => Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()), } } }

A broker's per-message settings, such as a priority, a QoS or a key: defaulted by the publish policy, set per publish by the broker's own steps. A broker declares its settings as Publisher::Options, a type of its own with every field optional. The publish policy at the mount site holds the defaults. A body that sets one bounds its slot Out<impl Publisher<Options = ..>, _> and imports the broker's prelude, whose extension trait adds the steps to the builder. A step sets one field for one publish; a field no step touches keeps the policy's default. A reply and a retry copy have no call site, so a transform that writes the broker's options sets them there. A transform runs after the call site, so it wins a field both of them set. A setting reaches the broker's publisher as a value, not as a header, and a test reads it back with with_options. The memory broker's publisher has no settings, so the example wraps it with a priority the way a networked broker ships one, and turns the priority into a header the test can read. A service on a networked broker imports the broker's own options and steps instead.

The body sets the priority of an express order; the mount site sets the default. Macros Manual examples/per_message_options.rs /// The bound names the broker's settings, so the broker's own steps appear on the builder. #[subscriber("orders")] async fn ship( order: &Order, Out(out): Out<impl Publisher<Options = PriorityOptions>, Shipments>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { let shipment = out.message(order).to("shipments"); let sent = if order.express { shipment.priority(9).publish().await } else { shipment.publish().await }; if sent.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/per_message_options.rs /// The bound names the broker's settings, so the broker's own steps appear on the builder. struct Ship; impl<Entry> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Entry,)>> for Ship where Entry: OutEntry<Shipments, Wire: Publisher<Options = PriorityOptions>>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Entry,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let shipment = outs.get(Shipments).message(order).to("shipments"); let sent = if order.express { shipment.priority(9).publish().await } else { shipment.publish().await }; if sent.is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(()) } } A reply takes its settings from a transform. Macros Manual examples/per_message_options.rs /// A reply has no call site, so a transform sets its settings. struct LowPriority; impl<K: ContextKind> PublishTransform<K, PriorityOptions> for LowPriority { type Destination = Reads; fn apply( &self, _out: &mut Outgoing<'_>, options: &mut Option<PriorityOptions>, _cx: &K::View<'_>, ) { options .get_or_insert_with(PriorityOptions::default) .priority = Some(1); } } #[subscriber("receipt-requests", reply)] async fn issue_receipt(order: &Order) -> Receipt { Receipt { order_id: order.id } } examples/manual/per_message_options.rs /// A reply has no call site, so a transform sets its settings. struct LowPriority; impl<K: ContextKind> PublishTransform<K, PriorityOptions> for LowPriority { type Destination = Reads; fn apply( &self, _out: &mut Outgoing<'_>, options: &mut Option<PriorityOptions>, _cx: &K::View<'_>, ) { options .get_or_insert_with(PriorityOptions::default) .priority = Some(1); } } struct IssueReceipt; impl Handle<Order, Receipt> for IssueReceipt { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Receipt, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(Receipt { order_id: order.id })) } } Macros Manual examples/per_message_options.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { // The policy holds the defaults: priority 3 unless a step says otherwise. b.include(ship) .out(Shipments, PriorityPublish::default().priority(3)) .include(issue_receipt) .out_reply(PriorityPublish::default().priority(3)) .transform(LowPriority) }) } examples/manual/per_message_options.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { // The policy holds the defaults: priority 3 unless a step says otherwise. b.include(subscriber("orders", Ship).build()) .out(Shipments, PriorityPublish::default().priority(3)) .include(subscriber("receipt-requests", IssueReceipt).reply().build()) .out_reply(PriorityPublish::default().priority(3)) .transform(LowPriority) }) }

The publisher capabilities a broker offers, one trait each, starting with Publisher. A handler names the capability its slot needs, never the broker's publisher type. A slot bound to a policy whose live publisher lacks that capability does not compile. A broker offers only the capabilities its transport has: Kafka-like brokers carry one transaction per producer, and request and reply need a broker that correlates answers.

OwnedTransactions opens independent transactions that own their buffers, so a handler keeps several open on one slot at once. A broker whose transactions are client buffers flushed at commit offers this kind: an AMQP confirms buffer, a Redis pipeline, the memory broker. A handler bounds its slot Out<impl OwnedTransactions, Marker> and calls transaction(). Each call returns a TypedTransaction of its own, and settling one never touches another. Publishes go through the transaction's builder and stay in its buffer until commit() flushes them together. commit() and abort() consume the value, so a publish after settling does not compile. A transaction dropped unsettled discards its buffer, the way an abort does, and logs a warning. The transaction sends from its own buffer: the slot's transforms and the app's publish layers do not run on its messages, and a test reads them on the destination record, published, rather than the slot's. Kafka-like brokers offer only the borrowed kind, TransactionalPublisher.

A transfer books its entries in one transaction and its audit record in another, so an empty transfer keeps the audit record and books nothing. Macros Manual examples/owned_transactions.rs #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Debit, Credit, Audited)] struct Ledger; /// The audit record and the entries settle apart: two transactions open on one slot. #[subscriber("transfers")] async fn book( transfer: &Transfer, Out(ledger): Out<impl OwnedTransactions, Ledger>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { let Ok(mut audit) = ledger.transaction().await else { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); }; let Ok(mut entries) = ledger.transaction().await else { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); }; let id = transfer.id; if audit.message(&Audited { id }).publish().await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } if transfer.amount == 0 { // Nothing to book: the entries go, the audit record stays. if entries.abort().await.is_err() || audit.commit().await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } return HandlerOutcome::ack(); } let amount = transfer.amount; let debit = entries.message(&Debit { id, amount }).publish().await; let credit = entries.message(&Credit { id, amount }).publish().await; if debit.is_err() || credit.is_err() || entries.commit().await.is_err() || audit.commit().await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/owned_transactions.rs struct Ledger; impl OutSlot for Ledger { const NAME: &'static str = "Ledger"; type Destination = Reads; } impl PublishedThrough<Ledger> for Debit {} impl PublishedThrough<Ledger> for Credit {} impl PublishedThrough<Ledger> for Audited {} /// The audit record and the entries settle apart: two transactions open on one slot. struct Book; impl<L> Handle<Transfer, (), Outs<(L,)>> for Book where L: OutEntry<Ledger, Wire: OwnedTransactions>, { async fn handle( &self, transfer: &Transfer, outs: &Outs<(L,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let ledger = outs.get(Ledger); let Ok(mut audit) = ledger.transaction().await else { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); }; let Ok(mut entries) = ledger.transaction().await else { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); }; let id = transfer.id; if audit.message(&Audited { id }).publish().await.is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } if transfer.amount == 0 { // Nothing to book: the entries go, the audit record stays. if entries.abort().await.is_err() || audit.commit().await.is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } return Ok(()); } let amount = transfer.amount; let debit = entries.message(&Debit { id, amount }).publish().await; let credit = entries.message(&Credit { id, amount }).publish().await; if debit.is_err() || credit.is_err() || entries.commit().await.is_err() || audit.commit().await.is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(()) } } Macros Manual examples/owned_transactions.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("ledger", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(book).out(Ledger, Publish) }) } examples/manual/owned_transactions.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("ledger", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("transfers", Book).build()) .out(Ledger, Publish) }) }

Publisher is the capability every slot names; a publish policy at the mount site becomes one when startup pairs it with the connected broker. A handler bounds its slot on the capability, Out<impl Publisher>, and never on a broker's publisher type. The same handler then mounts on a production broker and on its in-process test transport unchanged. A policy holds no connection, so it is built anywhere: a broker's prelude names its plain one Publish. Startup pairs each policy with the connected broker, so a handler never holds a publisher that is not connected. A reply with no policy named leaves through the broker's default one, DefaultPublish. A startup hook such as after_startup takes a policy and gets its live publisher, for a publish outside any handler. A bare publisher starts a publish with the same builder, under the default codec. A publisher declares three types. Payload says how its client takes the bytes: Lend when it only reads them, so the runtime lends one reused buffer, and Take when it keeps them. Options are its per-message settings, and Error is what a failed publish returns. Its base_headers go on every message it sends, under the headers of the call site. The narrower capabilities extend it: TransactionalPublisher, OwnedTransactions and RequestReply.

The handler names the capability; the mount site and the startup hook name the policy. Macros Manual examples/publisher.rs /// The bound names a capability, never the broker's publisher type. #[subscriber("orders")] async fn archive(order: &Order, Out(out): Out<impl Publisher>) -> HandlerOutcome { if out .message(order) .to("orders.archive") .publish() .await .is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/publisher.rs /// The bound names a capability, never the broker's publisher type. struct Archive; impl<Egress> Handle<Order, (), Outs<(Egress,)>> for Archive where Egress: OutEntry<DefaultSlot, Wire: Publisher>, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(Egress,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { if outs .get(DefaultSlot) .message(order) .to("orders.archive") .publish() .await .is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } Ok(()) } } Macros Manual examples/publisher.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("archive", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { // A startup hook gets the live publisher of the policy it names. b.after_startup(Publish, async move |publisher| { publisher .message(&Started { service: "archive".into(), }) .publish() .await }) // A policy holds no connection; startup pairs it with the connected broker. .include(archive) .out(DefaultSlot, Publish) }) } examples/manual/publisher.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("archive", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { // A startup hook gets the live publisher of the policy it names. b.after_startup(Publish, async move |publisher| { publisher .message(&Started { service: "archive".into(), }) .publish() .await }) // A policy holds no connection; startup pairs it with the connected broker. .include(subscriber("orders", Archive).build()) .out(DefaultSlot, Publish) }) }

RequestReply sends a request from a handler and awaits the correlated answer, on a broker that correlates replies natively. NATS-style brokers correlate replies, and the memory broker does too; Kafka and classic queues do not offer this capability. A handler bounds its slot Out<impl RequestReply, Marker>, and the mount site binds the broker's request policy, which its prelude names Request. request(message, timeout) publishes the message and resolves on the first answer, or fails once the time runs out. The request is an OutgoingMessage of bytes the handler encoded, and the answer is the broker's incoming message, which the handler decodes. The request goes to the broker directly, past the slot's transforms and the app's publish layers. The broker names an inbox for the answer: the memory broker puts it in the reply-to header. The responder is an ordinary reply handler whose reply goes to that inbox, through a naming transform. The slot also publishes with the builder, what its #[publishes(..)] list admits.

The handler asks the quote service for a price, then publishes the priced order through the same slot. Macros Manual examples/requester.rs #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Priced)] struct Pricing; #[subscriber("orders")] async fn price(order: &Order, Out(pricing): Out) -> HandlerOutcome { let Ok(ask) = serde_json::to_vec(&Ask { id: order.id }) else { return HandlerOutcome::drop(); }; let request = OutgoingMessage::new("quotes.ask", ask.as_slice()); let Ok(answer) = pricing.request(request, Duration::from_secs(2)).await else { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); }; let Ok(quote) = serde_json::from_slice::(answer.payload()) else { return HandlerOutcome::drop(); }; let priced = Priced { id: order.id, price: quote.price, }; if pricing.message(&priced).publish().await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/requester.rs struct Pricing; impl OutSlot for Pricing { const NAME: &'static str = "Pricing"; type Destination = Reads; } impl PublishedThrough for Priced {} struct Price; impl

Handle> for Price where P: OutEntry, { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, outs: &Outs<(P,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let pricing = outs.get(Pricing); let ask = serde_json::to_vec(&Ask { id: order.id }).map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::drop())?; let request = OutgoingMessage::new("quotes.ask", ask.as_slice()); let answer = pricing .request(request, Duration::from_secs(2)) .await .map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry())?; let quote = serde_json::from_slice::(answer.payload()) .map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::drop())?; let priced = Priced { id: order.id, price: quote.price, }; pricing .message(&priced) .publish() .await .map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry()) } } The responder answers on the inbox the request named. Macros Manual examples/requester.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { // The broker's request policy: its live publisher correlates replies. b.include(price) .out(Pricing, Request) .include(quote_price) .out_reply(Publish) .transform(ToInbox) }) } examples/manual/requester.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("orders", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { // The broker's request policy: its live publisher correlates replies. b.include(subscriber("orders", Price).build()) .out(Pricing, Request) .include( subscriber("quotes.ask", QuoteAsk) .reply() .to("quotes.answers") .build(), ) .out_reply(Publish) .transform(ToInbox) }) }

TransactionalPublisher puts several publishes in one broker transaction: every reply of a batch, or a scope a handler opens on its slot. Messages published inside a transaction become visible together on commit, or not at all. A batch handler whose reply chain ends with .transactional() publishes every reply of the batch in one transaction, and acks the batch after the commit. A policy whose live publisher has no transactions does not compile there. A broker's prelude names its transactional policy TransactionalPublish. By hand, a handler bounds its slot Out<impl TransactionalPublisher, Marker> and calls begin(). It returns a TransactionScope that owns the transaction, and publishes go through the scope's builder. commit() and abort() consume the scope, so a second commit or a publish after settling does not compile. A scope dropped unsettled logs a warning and leaves the broker transaction open, so a handler settles every scope it opens. The scope sends straight into the transaction: the slot's transforms and the app's publish layers do not run on its messages. This is the borrowed kind of transaction: the publisher carries one broker transaction, and one scope is open on it at a time. Kafka-like brokers, whose client holds one transaction per producer, offer this kind only. Brokers whose transactions are client buffers also offer OwnedTransactions.

Every confirmation of a batch in one transaction. Macros Manual examples/transactional_publisher.rs /// Every confirmation of a batch becomes visible at once, on commit. #[subscriber("orders", reply)] async fn confirm(orders: &[Order]) -> Vec<Confirmed> { orders .iter() .map(|order| Confirmed { id: order.id }) .collect() } examples/manual/transactional_publisher.rs /// Every confirmation of a batch becomes visible at once, on commit. struct Confirm; impl Handle<[Order], Vec<Confirmed>> for Confirm { fn handle( &self, orders: &[Order], _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Vec<Confirmed>, Vec<HandlerOutcome>>> { ready(Ok(orders .iter() .map(|order| Confirmed { id: order.id }) .collect())) } } A scope opened on a slot: both entries of a payment, or neither. Macros Manual examples/transactional_publisher.rs #[derive(OutSlot)] #[publishes(Debit, Credit)] struct Ledger; /// Both entries of a payment, or neither. #[subscriber("payments")] async fn book( payment: &Payment, Out(ledger): Out<impl TransactionalPublisher, Ledger>, ) -> HandlerOutcome { let Ok(scope) = ledger.begin().await else { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); }; let (id, amount) = (payment.id, payment.amount); let debit = scope.message(&Debit { id, amount }).publish().await; let credit = scope.message(&Credit { id, amount }).publish().await; if debit.is_err() || credit.is_err() { if let Err(err) = scope.abort().await { tracing::warn!(payment.id, %err, "payments: aborting the ledger transaction failed"); } return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } match scope.commit().await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(_) => HandlerOutcome::retry(), } } examples/manual/transactional_publisher.rs struct Ledger; impl OutSlot for Ledger { const NAME: &'static str = "Ledger"; type Destination = Reads; } impl PublishedThrough<Ledger> for Debit {} impl PublishedThrough<Ledger> for Credit {} /// Both entries of a payment, or neither. struct Book; impl<L> Handle<Payment, (), Outs<(L,)>> for Book where L: OutEntry<Ledger, Wire: TransactionalPublisher>, { async fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, outs: &Outs<(L,)>, _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let Ok(scope) = outs.get(Ledger).begin().await else { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); }; let (id, amount) = (payment.id, payment.amount); let debit = scope.message(&Debit { id, amount }).publish().await; let credit = scope.message(&Credit { id, amount }).publish().await; if debit.is_err() || credit.is_err() { if let Err(err) = scope.abort().await { tracing::warn!(payment.id, %err, "payments: aborting the ledger transaction failed"); } return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } scope.commit().await.map_err(|_| HandlerOutcome::retry()) } } Macros Manual examples/transactional_publisher.rs fn app(broker: MemoryBroker) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("ledger", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // One transaction per batch, committed before the batch is acked. b.include(confirm.batch(nonzero!(64))) .out_reply(TransactionalPublish) .transactional() .include(book) .out(Ledger, TransactionalPublish) }) } examples/manual/transactional_publisher.rs fn app(broker: MemoryBroker) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("ledger", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // One transaction per batch, committed before the batch is acked. b.include( subscriber("orders", Confirm) .reply() .batch(nonzero!(64)) .build(), ) .out_reply(TransactionalPublish) .transactional() .include(subscriber("payments", Book).build()) .out(Ledger, TransactionalPublish) }) }

A handler answers a message by returning a value; the reply type or the mount site says where the answer goes. Every reply type derives Outgoing. A type with #[outgoing(name = "..")] fixes its destination, and the handler carries the bare clause #[subscriber("src", reply)]. A type that names nothing takes the destination from the clause, reply("dest"). A destination declared on the type wins over a name at the mount site, and startup logs a warning for such a registration. The forms of a destination are on the Destinations page. Result<Reply, HandlerOutcome> keeps the settlement in the handler's hands: Ok publishes the reply and acks, Err publishes nothing and settles by the outcome. A reply whose publish fails nacks the delivery with requeue, so a replying handler has to be safe to run twice. A batch handler returns one Vec of replies per batch. With nothing else said, the reply leaves through the broker's default policy under the default codec. .out_reply(policy) names the publish policy, and the steps after it complete the reply's wiring. .codec(..) names the codec of the reply, while the request still decodes with the scope's codec. .transform(..) adds a publish transform, and .transactional() puts every reply of a batch in one broker transaction. A broker that only reads the payload is lent the dispatch loop's own encode buffer, so a reply allocates nothing per delivery.

The reply type fixes its destination. Macros Manual examples/replies.rs /// The reply type fixes its destination, so the clause is the bare `reply`. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "receipts")] struct Receipt { order_id: u64, } /// `Ok` publishes the receipt and acks; `Err` publishes nothing and settles by the outcome. #[subscriber("orders", reply)] async fn issue_receipt(order: &Order) -> Result<Receipt, HandlerOutcome> { if order.id == 0 { return Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()); } Ok(Receipt { order_id: order.id }) } examples/manual/replies.rs /// The reply type fixes its destination, so the chain names none. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, schemars::JsonSchema)] struct Receipt { order_id: u64, } // `#[outgoing(name = "receipts")]` by hand. impl OutgoingDestination for Receipt { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "receipts"; } impl MessageHeaders for Receipt { type Contract = NoHeaders; } /// `Ok` publishes the receipt and acks; `Err` publishes nothing and settles by the outcome. struct IssueReceipt; impl Handle<Order, Receipt> for IssueReceipt { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Receipt, HandlerOutcome>> { if order.id == 0 { return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::drop())); } ready(Ok(Receipt { order_id: order.id })) } } The clause names the destination of a type that declares none. Macros Manual examples/replies.rs /// The reply type declares no destination, so the clause names one. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] struct Quote { order_id: u64, price: u64, } #[subscriber("quote-requests", reply("quotes"))] async fn quote(order: &Order) -> Quote { Quote { order_id: order.id, price: order.id * 10, } } examples/manual/replies.rs /// The reply type declares no destination, so the chain names one. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, schemars::JsonSchema)] struct Quote { order_id: u64, price: u64, } impl OutgoingDestination for Quote { type Form = CallerName; } impl MessageHeaders for Quote { type Contract = NoHeaders; } struct QuoteOrder; impl Handle<Order, Quote> for QuoteOrder { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Quote, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(Quote { order_id: order.id, price: order.id * 10, })) } } Macros Manual examples/replies.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { // The broker's default policy, under the default codec. b.include(issue_receipt) // The policy the reply leaves through, named at the mount site. .include(quote) .out_reply(Publish) }) } examples/manual/replies.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { // The broker's default policy, under the default codec. b.include(subscriber("orders", IssueReceipt).reply().build()) // The destination the type leaves open, and the policy the reply leaves through. .include( subscriber("quote-requests", QuoteOrder) .reply() .to("quotes") .build(), ) .out_reply(Publish) }) }

A publish transform changes an outgoing message at one publish position, before it reaches the publisher. A transform belongs to one position: a reply, one slot, or the replies of a batch. It is static, so the chain of transforms is one type and costs only its own code. What it reads, which settings it writes and whether it names the destination are part of its type, so a transform mounted where it does not fit does not compile. The app-wide counterpart, which wraps every publish of the app, is the publish layer.

A batch publish transform is a step on the replies of a batch handler: each reply passes it on its own, with the batch's context. A batch handler with a reply returns one Vec of replies per batch, and those replies pass their own steps. .batch_transform(..) adds one after .out_reply(policy), and a single-message mount rejects it at compile time. The per-message publish transforms do not run on batch replies, and batch transforms do not run on single replies. for_batch lifts a per-message transform onto the batch path, so one impl serves both. All replies of a batch see one PublishContext, the batch's: its name is the subscription, its headers are empty, and its context fields are the broker's batch context. A transform that reads the message it answers belongs on a single-message handler. A batch reply never offers the naming right. A batch transform has no macro form: the same impl serves both forms, and only the mounting differs.

examples/batch_transform.rs /// Marks every reply of a batch. It sees the batch's context, not one delivery's. struct Batched; impl<C, Options> BatchPublishTransform<C, Options> for Batched { fn apply( &self, out: &mut Outgoing<'_>, _options: &mut Option<Options>, _cx: &PublishContext<'_, C>, ) { out.headers_mut().insert("batched", "true"); } } /// A per-message transform, reused on the batch path through `for_batch`. struct Service(&'static str); impl<K: ContextKind, Options> PublishTransform<K, Options> for Service { type Destination = Reads; fn apply(&self, out: &mut Outgoing<'_>, _options: &mut Option<Options>, _cx: &K::View<'_>) { out.headers_mut().insert("service", self.0); } } Macros Manual examples/batch_transform.rs fn app(broker: MemoryBroker) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(confirm.batch(nonzero!(64))) .out_reply(Publish) .batch_transform(Batched) .batch_transform(for_batch(Service("billing"))) }) } examples/manual/batch_transform.rs fn app(broker: MemoryBroker) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include( subscriber("orders", Confirm) .reply() .to("receipts") .batch(nonzero!(64)) .build(), ) .out_reply(Publish) .batch_transform(Batched) .batch_transform(for_batch(Service("billing"))) }) }

A naming transform sets the destination of each message, on a position where nothing else declared it: a reply to the inbox a request named. A transform that declares type Destination = Names may call set_name on the outgoing message. A position offers that right only where nothing declared the destination: a reply type with no #[outgoing(name = ..)], or a slot whose whole #[publishes(..)] list leaves it open. It offers it once, so a second naming transform on one position does not compile, and neither does one on a declared reply or on a batch reply. DefaultSlot and a slot that lists a declared destination never offer it. The name at the mount site stays the declared fallback: the generated document reports it, and a delivery the transform leaves alone is answered there. A name read off the delivery costs no copy: get_shared hands over the header's own buffer, and Str checks it is UTF-8. The reply side of RequestReply is the usual case. A naming transform is a publish transform in every other way: it has no macro form, and only the mounting differs.

examples/naming_transform.rs /// Answers on the inbox the question named in its `reply-to` header. The header's bytes become /// the destination as they are: one UTF-8 check, no copy. struct ToInbox; impl<C, Options> PublishTransform<ForReply<C>, Options> for ToInbox { type Destination = Names; fn apply( &self, out: &mut Outgoing<'_>, _options: &mut Option<Options>, cx: &PublishContext<'_, C>, ) { if let Some(inbox) = cx.headers().get_shared("reply-to") && let Ok(name) = Str::try_from(inbox) { out.set_name(name); } } } Macros Manual examples/naming_transform.rs /// `"answers"` is the fallback, and what the generated document reports. #[subscriber("questions", reply("answers"))] async fn answer(question: &Question) -> Answer { Answer { id: question.id } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("answers", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(answer).out_reply(Publish).transform(ToInbox) }) } examples/manual/naming_transform.rs struct AnswerQuestion; impl Handle<Question, Answer> for AnswerQuestion { fn handle( &self, question: &Question, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<Answer, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(Answer { id: question.id })) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("answers", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { // `"answers"` is the fallback, and what the generated document reports. b.include( subscriber("questions", AnswerQuestion) .reply() .to("answers") .build(), ) .out_reply(Publish) .transform(ToInbox) }) }

A publish transform is a static step on one publish position: it reads the delivery or the slot, and changes the outgoing message. .transform(..) adds one after the position it belongs to: after .out_reply(policy) for a reply, after .out(marker, policy) for a slot. Its apply gets the outgoing message, the broker's per-message settings and a view of the position, and returns nothing: it cannot refuse a publish. An impl declares three things. The kind is what it reads. ForReply<C> reads the delivery being answered through a PublishContext: its channel, headers and the broker's context fields. ForSlot reads a SlotContext, the slot's name and nothing else, because the body that publishes has already read its delivery. The Options parameter is the settings it writes: (), or the broker's own type, which mounts it only over that broker's publisher. type Destination is what it may do to the destination: Reads leaves it alone, and Names sets it. A transform that reads and sets nothing is generic over both, impl<K: ContextKind, Options>, and mounts anywhere. Transforms run in the order the chain writes them, then the app's publish layers, then the send. The chain is one type, built when the code compiles, so a transform costs only its own code. A reply of a batch handler takes batch transforms instead. A transform has no macro form: the same impl serves both forms, and only the mounting differs.

A reply transform carries the request's correlation id onto the reply. examples/publish_transform.rs /// Carries the request's correlation id onto its reply. `ForReply` reads the delivery being /// answered, so this transform mounts on a reply position. struct Correlate; impl<C, Options> PublishTransform<ForReply<C>, Options> for Correlate { type Destination = Reads; fn apply( &self, out: &mut Outgoing<'_>, _options: &mut Option<Options>, cx: &PublishContext<'_, C>, ) { // The delivery's own buffer, shared rather than copied. if let Some(id) = cx.headers().get_shared("correlation-id") { out.headers_mut().insert("correlation-id", id); } } } A slot transform stamps a constant on what leaves the slot. examples/publish_transform.rs /// Stamps the schema version on what leaves a slot. `ForSlot` reads the slot's name and nothing /// else: the body that publishes has already read its delivery. struct SchemaVersion(&'static str); impl<Options> PublishTransform<ForSlot, Options> for SchemaVersion { type Destination = Reads; fn apply(&self, out: &mut Outgoing<'_>, _options: &mut Option<Options>, _cx: &SlotContext<'_>) { out.headers_mut().insert("schema-version", self.0); } } Macros Manual examples/publish_transform.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { // A transform follows the position it belongs to. b.include(confirm) .out_reply(Publish) .transform(Correlate) .include(audit) .out(Trail, Publish) .transform(SchemaVersion("2")) }) } examples/manual/publish_transform.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { // A transform follows the position it belongs to. b.include(subscriber("orders", Confirm).reply().to("receipts").build()) .out_reply(Publish) .transform(Correlate) .include(subscriber("payments", AuditPayment).build()) .out(Trail, Publish) .transform(SchemaVersion("2")) }) }
A subscription over a replayable log opens at a position of your choice, and its handler can move it.

A handler moves its own subscription to another position of the log through the broker's seek handle. The in-memory broker's per-delivery context carries the handle under the key SeekHandle. A handler reads it with the Ctx<SeekHandle> parameter; the manual form declares MemoryContext on its Handle and reads ctx.context(SeekHandle). seek takes a MemoryPosition, the same type start_at takes. Once seek resolves, the next delivery comes from the new position, and entries already queued before it are skipped. A sequence the retention bound has already evicted is refused with an error, and the example retries the delivery then. The handle implements Seeker, the trait a broker with a replayable log provides. Ctx<SeekHandle> does not compile against MemoryBroker::new(), which keeps no log.

The handler meets a poison marker and moves its subscription past the entries behind it. Macros Manual examples/seek.rs /// The id that marks a poisoned region: the entries up to the resume point are skipped. const POISON: u64 = 999; #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "jobs")] struct Job { id: u64, } /// The seek handle is a field of the broker's per-delivery context, read with `Ctx`. #[subscriber("jobs", start_at(MemoryPosition::start()))] async fn work(job: &Job, Ctx(seeker): Ctx<SeekHandle>) -> HandlerOutcome { if job.id == POISON { // Resume at the fourth entry of the log. if seeker.seek(MemoryPosition::sequence(3)).await.is_err() { return HandlerOutcome::retry(); } return HandlerOutcome::ack(); } tracing::info!(job.id, "processed"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/seek.rs /// The id that marks a poisoned region: the entries up to the resume point are skipped. const POISON: u64 = 999; #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, schemars::JsonSchema)] struct Job { id: u64, } // `#[outgoing(name = "jobs")]` by hand: the type fixes its destination. impl OutgoingDestination for Job { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "jobs"; } impl MessageHeaders for Job { type Contract = NoHeaders; } struct Work; // Declaring the broker's `MemoryContext` is what puts the seek handle in the context. impl Handle<Job, (), (), MemoryContext> for Work { async fn handle( &self, job: &Job, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, MemoryContext>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { if job.id == POISON { // Resume at the fourth entry of the log. let seeker = ctx.context(SeekHandle); if seeker.seek(MemoryPosition::sequence(3)).await.is_err() { return Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()); } return Ok(()); } tracing::info!(job.id, "processed"); Ok(()) } } fn app(broker: MemoryBroker<Retaining>) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("jobs", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include( subscriber("jobs", Work) .start_at(MemoryPosition::start()) .build(), ) }) }

start_at opens a replayable subscription at a position: the start of the log, a sequence number, or the tip. A broker over a replayable log owns its position type; for the in-memory broker it is MemoryPosition. start_at(position) seeks the subscription before its first delivery, on every startup. It is one of the mount-site settings, and the attribute takes it as a clause too. Without it, the subscription opens at the broker's default; the in-memory broker's default is the tip of the log, so earlier entries are not delivered. MemoryPosition::start() is the oldest entry the broker still keeps, sequence(n) the n-th entry published to the name, counted from zero, and end() the tip. The in-memory broker keeps a log only when it is built with MemoryBroker::retaining. start_at does not compile against MemoryBroker::new(), which keeps nothing. A broker's subscription accepts a position when it implements Seekable.

The subscription opens at the start of the log and replays what was published before the service started. Macros Manual examples/seek.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, Outgoing)] #[outgoing(name = "audit")] struct Entry { id: u64, } /// The audit trail opens at the start of the log, so it also reads what came before it. #[subscriber("audit", start_at(MemoryPosition::start()))] async fn record(entry: &Entry) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(entry.id, "recorded"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// Replaying reads what the broker kept, so this one keeps the last 64 entries of every name. /// `MemoryBroker::new()` keeps nothing, and a mount that seeks does not compile on it. fn broker() -> MemoryBroker<Retaining> { MemoryBroker::retaining(Retention::Messages(nonzero!(64))) } examples/manual/seek.rs #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Deserialize, Serialize, schemars::JsonSchema)] struct Entry { id: u64, } // `#[outgoing(name = "audit")]` by hand: the type fixes its destination. impl OutgoingDestination for Entry { type Form = FixedName; const DESTINATION: &'static str = "audit"; } impl MessageHeaders for Entry { type Contract = NoHeaders; } struct Record; impl Handle<Entry> for Record { fn handle( &self, entry: &Entry, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(entry.id, "recorded"); ready(Ok(())) } } /// Replaying reads what the broker kept, so this one keeps the last 64 entries of every name. /// `MemoryBroker::new()` keeps nothing, and a mount that seeks does not compile on it. fn broker() -> MemoryBroker<Retaining> { MemoryBroker::retaining(Retention::Messages(nonzero!(64))) } fn app(broker: MemoryBroker<Retaining>) -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("audit", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { // The audit trail opens at the start of the log, so it also reads what came before it. b.include( subscriber("audit", Record) .start_at(MemoryPosition::start()) .build(), ) }) }

max_attempts(n) ends a message that keeps coming back, and dead_letter(name) is where it goes then. max_attempts(n) counts the deliveries one message gets, the first one included. The delivery that reaches the cap is not retried: it is published to the dead_letter destination with its payload and headers. A cap without a destination rejects the delivery instead, and a warning names the subscription. The count is the broker's own where the transport keeps one, read through redelivery_count, and the framework's RETRY_COUNT_HEADER where it keeps none. The in-memory broker counts its deliveries, so the cap there counts its redeliveries. A retry() and a retry_after(delay) are both capped. Where the broker moves a spent delivery itself (a queue with a delivery limit and a dead-letter exchange), the declaration reaches the subscription descriptor at startup, and the broker applies it. The two steps come right after include, before .out_retry(..), the slot the dead-letter copy leaves through, and each is written once.

Macros Manual examples/retry.rs /// The gateway rejects this payment every time, so on its own it would never stop coming back. #[subscriber("payments")] async fn charge(payment: &Payment) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::warn!(payment.id, "gateway refused the charge"); HandlerOutcome::retry() } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { // Three deliveries, then the payment goes to the dead-letter subject. b.include(charge) .max_attempts(nonzero!(3u32)) .dead_letter("payments.dead") }) } examples/manual/retry.rs /// The gateway rejects this payment every time, so on its own it would never stop coming back. struct Charge; impl Handle<Payment> for Charge { fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::warn!(payment.id, "gateway refused the charge"); ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { // Three deliveries, then the payment goes to the dead-letter subject. b.include(subscriber("payments", Charge).build()) .max_attempts(nonzero!(3u32)) .dead_letter("payments.dead") }) }

The Retry slot is the publisher a copy of a delivery leaves through; .out_retry(policy) replaces it and .to(name) names its destination. The runtime publishes a copy of a delivery in two cases: a delayed retry_after on a broker without native delayed redelivery, and a delivery sent to its dead_letter destination. Every registration has a publisher for those copies, paired from the broker's default publish policy. .out_retry(policy) replaces it; it is the Out slot Retry, so .codec(..) and .transform(..) follow it as on any slot. A copy carries the delivery's own bytes, so no codec encodes it, and its PublishTransforms read the delivery being retried. A copy sent back to the subscription carries the RETRY_COUNT_HEADER, incremented. On the in-memory broker the delay is native, so only the dead-letter copy leaves through this slot. A subscription whose source descriptor declares AddressedCopies reports where it is reached again, and copies go there. One that declares NamedCopies reads many destinations and addresses none: a wildcard, a filter, a pattern. On it the mount site names the destination with .to(name), or a transform names one per delivery. Without either, a router chain does not compile, and a mount in a broker scope refuses to start. A name given with .to(name) is a channel the registration sends to, and the generated document reports it. A broker that moves a spent delivery itself declares BrokerMoves, and .out_retry(..) does not compile there.

Macros Manual examples/settle_retry_destination.rs /// Stamps every copy with the subscription its delivery came from. struct RetriedFrom; impl<C, Options> PublishTransform<ForReply<C>, Options> for RetriedFrom { type Destination = Reads; fn apply( &self, out: &mut Outgoing<'_>, _options: &mut Option<Options>, cx: &PublishContext<'_, C>, ) { out.headers_mut() .insert("x-retried-from", cx.name().to_owned()); } } #[subscriber("payments")] async fn charge(payment: &Payment) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::warn!(payment.id, "gateway refused the charge"); HandlerOutcome::retry() } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(charge) .max_attempts(nonzero!(2u32)) .dead_letter("payments.dead") // Replaces the broker's default publisher for the copies of this registration. .out_retry(Publish) .transform(RetriedFrom) }) } examples/manual/settle_retry_destination.rs /// Stamps every copy with the subscription its delivery came from. struct RetriedFrom; impl<C, Options> PublishTransform<ForReply<C>, Options> for RetriedFrom { type Destination = Reads; fn apply( &self, out: &mut Outgoing<'_>, _options: &mut Option<Options>, cx: &PublishContext<'_, C>, ) { out.headers_mut() .insert("x-retried-from", cx.name().to_owned()); } } struct Charge; impl Handle<Payment> for Charge { fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::warn!(payment.id, "gateway refused the charge"); ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry())) } } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("payments", Charge).build()) .max_attempts(nonzero!(2u32)) .dead_letter("payments.dead") // Replaces the broker's default publisher for the copies of this registration. .out_retry(Publish) .transform(RetriedFrom) }) }

Macros Manual examples/settle_retry_destination.rs /// A subscription that reads every payment subject and addresses none of them, as a wildcard /// or a topic filter does. `Copies = NamedCopies` says so. #[derive(Debug, Clone)] struct PaymentFilter { pattern: &'static str, } impl PaymentFilter { const fn new(pattern: &'static str) -> Self { Self { pattern } } } impl SubscriptionSource<ConnectedMemoryBroker> for PaymentFilter { type Subscriber = MemorySubscriber<Discarding>; type Copies = NamedCopies; fn name(&self) -> &str { self.pattern } async fn subscribe( self, connected: &ConnectedMemoryBroker, ) -> Result<Self::Subscriber, MemoryError> { MemoryPattern::new(self.pattern).subscribe(connected).await } } #[subscriber(PaymentFilter::new("payments.*"))] async fn reconcile(payment: &Payment) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(payment.id, "not cleared yet"); HandlerOutcome::retry_after(Duration::from_secs(5)) } examples/manual/settle_retry_destination.rs /// A subscription that reads every payment subject and addresses none of them, as a wildcard /// or a topic filter does. `Copies = NamedCopies` says so. #[derive(Debug, Clone)] struct PaymentFilter { pattern: &'static str, } impl PaymentFilter { const fn new(pattern: &'static str) -> Self { Self { pattern } } } impl SubscriptionSource<ConnectedMemoryBroker> for PaymentFilter { type Subscriber = MemorySubscriber<Discarding>; type Copies = NamedCopies; fn name(&self) -> &str { self.pattern } async fn subscribe( self, connected: &ConnectedMemoryBroker, ) -> Result<Self::Subscriber, MemoryError> { MemoryPattern::new(self.pattern).subscribe(connected).await } } // What `subscriber(..)` accepts as a source: the descriptor passes through as it is. impl IntoSource for PaymentFilter { type Source = Self; fn into_source(self) -> Self { self } } struct Reconcile; impl Handle<Payment> for Reconcile { fn handle( &self, payment: &Payment, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(payment.id, "not cleared yet"); ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after(Duration::from_secs(5)))) } } Macros Manual examples/settle_retry_destination.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { // The descriptor addresses nothing, so the mount site names where a copy goes. b.include(reconcile).out_retry(Publish).to("payments.retry") }) } /// The same registration with no destination named. fn unnamed() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| b.include(reconcile)) } examples/manual/settle_retry_destination.rs fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { // The descriptor addresses nothing, so the mount site names where a copy goes. b.include(subscriber(PaymentFilter::new("payments.*"), Reconcile).build()) .out_retry(Publish) .to("payments.retry") }) } /// The same registration with no destination named. fn unnamed() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber(PaymentFilter::new("payments.*"), Reconcile).build()) }) }

A Router groups one module's handlers with their own middleware and codec, and include_router mounts the group on a broker. A router is a group of registrations bound to a broker type, not to a broker value, so a module builds it without a connection. include adds a #[subscriber] handler to the router the same way it adds one to a broker scope, settings included. A router's full type names every registration in a RouterDef, so a builder function returns impl RouterDef<B>, or Router<B, impl RouterDef<B>> when the caller still merges it. merge appends another router's registrations, and each router keeps its own codec and layers. include_router on a broker scope of the application mounts the group, as a step of the scope's chain before its includes. layer adds middleware and is called before the router's first include; after one, .layer(..) applies to that registration alone. A router's layer must be a BlanketLayer, because the router hides its handlers' types. The app's own layers wrap outside the router's layers. Router layers wrap single-message handlers; batch handlers are not wrapped. with_codec switches the codec mid-chain: registrations already added keep the codec they were added with. Without it, a router decodes with the default codec, JSON when the json feature is on.

Each module returns its router, and the service merges them and mounts the result. Macros Manual examples/routing.rs #[subscriber("orders")] async fn accept(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "accepted"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[subscriber("shipments")] async fn dispatch(shipment: &Shipment) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(shipment.order_id, "dispatched"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// The orders module's handlers. fn orders() -> Router<MemoryBroker, impl RouterDef<MemoryBroker>> { Router::new().include(accept) } /// The shipping module's handlers. fn shipping() -> Router<MemoryBroker, impl RouterDef<MemoryBroker>> { Router::new().include(dispatch) } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shop", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include_router(orders().merge(shipping())) }) } examples/manual/routing.rs struct Accept; impl Handle<Order> for Accept { fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order.id, "accepted"); ready(Ok(())) } } struct Dispatch; impl Handle<Shipment> for Dispatch { fn handle( &self, shipment: &Shipment, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(shipment.order_id, "dispatched"); ready(Ok(())) } } /// The orders module's handlers. fn orders() -> Router<MemoryBroker, impl RouterDef<MemoryBroker>> { Router::new().include(subscriber("orders", Accept).build()) } /// The shipping module's handlers. fn shipping() -> Router<MemoryBroker, impl RouterDef<MemoryBroker>> { Router::new().include(subscriber("shipments", Dispatch).build()) } fn app() -> impl App { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shop", "0.1.0")).with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include_router(orders().merge(shipping())) }) }

Router::layer wraps every handler of the router, and nothing mounted outside it. Macros Manual examples/routing.rs /// Counts the deliveries of the handlers it wraps. #[derive(Clone)] struct Count(Arc<AtomicUsize>); struct Counted<H> { inner: H, count: Arc<AtomicUsize>, } // A router hides its handlers' types, so its layer wraps a handler of any type. impl BlanketLayer for Count { fn apply<M, C, S, H>(&self, handler: H) -> impl Handler<M, C, S> + 'static where M: Send + Sync + 'static, C: Send + 'static, S: Send + Sync + 'static, H: Handler<M, C, S> + 'static, { Counted { inner: handler, count: Arc::clone(&self.0), } } } impl<M, C, S, H> Handler<M, C, S> for Counted<H> where M: Send + Sync, C: Send, S: Send + Sync, H: Handler<M, C, S>, { async fn handle(&self, msg: &M, ctx: &mut Context<'_, C, S>) -> HandlerOutcome { self.count.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed); self.inner.handle(msg, ctx).await } } #[subscriber("orders")] async fn accept(order: &Order) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order.id, "accepted"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[subscriber("shipments")] async fn dispatch(shipment: &Shipment) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(shipment.order_id, "dispatched");
